#258. Jensen Huang pulls out of ElevenLabs Summit amid Nvidia controversy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pulled out of the ElevenLabs Summit scheduled for this Wednesday in New York, ElevenLabs, the voice AI company, confirmed Monday. He has also dropped out of other speaking engagements, including the Anthropic CEO Forum. Nvidia is an investor in ElevenLabs.

The withdrawals come after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and Nvidia opened an investigation into his relationship with a possible Chinese spy.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a memo to the company.

The incident has rattled the AI industry, raising questions about Huang’s staying power as CEO and Nvidia’s own China ambitions.

Ring is finally shipping a flying indoor drone camera. For real this time. The Ring Drone Cam will arrive on January 27th, 2027, for $249.99, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said at a launch event in New York City this week. If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced its first flying camera, the Ring Always Home Cam.

Designed to patrol inside your home when you’re not there, the Drone Cam is an AI-powered drone that can react to triggers from Ring sensors, such as detecting motion, a door opening, a water leak, or an alarm sounding. When triggered, it flies along preprogrammed routes to a set location, where it can livestream and record what’s happening in the Ring app.

The drone can also run scheduled patrols around your home or be sent out on demand. It offers 2K resolution, a 148-degree field of view, and, because it’s mobile, it can cover 360 degrees. The Verge got some hands-on time with the new flying camera at the launch event.

Ring’s pitch here is that the Drone Cam can replace the need for multiple cameras in your home while still letting you see what’s happening anywhere in your home if there’s an incident.

Footage from the Drone Cam is encrypted using Ring’s new TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption) system, which rotates encryption keys every five minutes and deletes Ring’s copies after 24 hours, limiting Amazon’s access while still allowing cloud processing for features like smart alerts and AI-powered video search.

At the event, I saw the Drone Cam take flight and got some hands-on time with the device. It’s a completely different product from the Always Home Cam that was announced in 2020. It’s significantly smaller, about a quarter the size of the model I saw demoed at CES in 2023, weighing 165 grams. A small camera is integrated into its body, as opposed to dangling in the center.

Ring claims the Drone Cam can fly for five to eight minutes on a charge, and for every minute of flight time, it takes eight minutes of charging — that means a five-minute flight needs about 40 minutes of charging. This short flight time suggests the product is better suited to quick check-ins than continuous monitoring, and whether it can really replace multiple stationary cameras remains to be seen.

At this week’s demo, I saw it complete a 1-minute flight, taking off from its dock, hovering, then following a pre-planned route around a simple living room layout. Unlike the CES demo, this time I was able to see the drone take off and land several times, then navigate smoothly with barely any wobble.

According to Ring, the Drone Cam can fly up stairs and uses LED spotlights to help it see in the dark and deter potential intruders — but Ring didn’t demo this. The drone apparently follows preplanned flight paths you set up in the Ring app and will go around any obstacles it encounters along those routes. However, I didn’t get to see it interact with obstacles or anything unexpected — I’m particularly curious how pets will react to it.

Siminoff said Ring has been developing the drone since 2016 and has come close to shipping two different models over that time before landing on the current version. Siminoff explained that they struggled to pack all the technology needed for an autonomous drone to fly in your home into a practical design for less than $250. About a year ago, they decided to start from scratch and build a much more basic drone that could fly reliably while putting its brains in the cloud.

Ring developed AI Pilot, a new AI system that combines the device’s camera with vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to map your home and let the drone navigate autonomously around obstacles, while relying on preprogrammed routes. “Truly, it’s like an AI agent that’s controlling the robot,” said Siminoff. The downside is that it depends entirely on an internet connection, which is a potential failure point for a home security product; without Wi-Fi, all it can do is land.

The Drone Cam launches in the US only as part of a new Ring Robotics line alongside the Ring Rover Cam, a $999.99 autonomous security robot for businesses built on Amazon’s Astro home robot. Rover also uses AI Pilot and is available for preorder now, with shipping expected to begin on December 16th, 2026.

Both security devices work like any other Ring camera, streaming and sending recorded video to the Ring app and requiring a Ring Protect plan for video storage and advanced features. They will also work with Amazon’s upcoming Alexa Home Map to understand your home and where sensors and other devices are located.

Although Siminoff seemed confident the drone will launch in January as planned, Ring says it is currently “in the process of obtaining FCC certification.” When asked about the FCC’s ban on foreign-made drones, Siminoff said Ring Drone Cam “does comply with” FCC regulations and noted it’s assembled in the US. It’s normal for new gadgets to go through this process, but drones now face extra scrutiny.

#255. Fervo now has $12B in orders for its geothermal power tech

Geothermal company Fervo couldn’t have picked a better time to deliver its first power plants.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released Monday, the company said it now has $11.9 billion worth of contracted revenue on the books, up from $7.2 billion last quarter.

Fervo has been hitting its deadlines recently, which undoubtedly has helped to drive orders.

As hyperscalers scour the earth for electricity to power their AI data centers, Fervo is on track to complete a 396 megawatt power plant for Google by the end of 2028. The geothermal company connected its first 100 megawatt power plant to the grid earlier this year.

Both projects are built at Cape Station in Utah, a resource that could generate 8.4 gigawatts of electricity. Previously, experts told Fervo the site could only produce about 4 gigawatts.

The Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, co-founder and CEO Tim Latimer said in an earnings call Monday. The arrangement means that Google can draw power from the deal and sell it to other customers if it’s not ready to use it.

“We built Cape Station on our schedule. Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule, and neither party is waiting on the other,” he said.

Latimer’s statement also underlines an advantage that geothermal has over competing generating sources like large nuclear or natural gas power plants — the phased nature of its construction.

Fervo’s newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of generating 15 megawatts gross power, and several are linked together into what the company calls a GeoBlock. The first completed GeoBlock generated 33 megawatts, while recent ones hit 50 megawatts. They’re sized to match the demand of a typical data center hall, so hyperscalers can bring them online as they’re completed.

As a business, Fervo is still in the early stages. It ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, though it holds cash and cash equivalents of $1.9 billion and long-term debt of $301.6 million, which should give it plenty of runway.

Much will depend on the company bringing down the cost of its power plants. While hyperscalers are hungry for power today, they may not always be as price-indiscriminate.

Yet if Fervo can deliver on its promises, it could end up winning on price. The first phase of its Cape Station project cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, the company said. The cost for its Google project is $5,500 per kilowatt, a significant drop that suggests Fervo is on the right path. With subsidies, that’s about equivalent to a new natural gas power plant running on fuel that costs $6 per million BTUs. Still about twice what natural gas costs today, but trending closer to where it needs to be.

But if Fervo can hit its long-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt, it could significantly undercut natural gas power, even at today’s prices. That’s a pretty ambitious target, but the company has made significant strides in just a few years. No wonder Google is getting in early.

#253. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

As part of a new brand called Ring Robotics — designed to take a more proactive approach to security instead of just monitoring — a new rolling mobile security camera was announced by Amazon, called the Ring Rover Cam. It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021. The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades.

As with Astro, the Rover Cam rolls around on a pair of large wheels that help it navigate small obstacles or uneven terrain. It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered. While en route, it continuously streams and records video, and when it reaches its destination, the robot performs a 360-degree scan so you can investigate what’s wrong from afar.

Astro’s extending periscope camera has been carried forward to the Rover Cam and upgraded. It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles. Astro’s cupholder has been replaced with a permanent stubby tower featuring a built-in siren and a flashing red light that both function as deterrents. To make the Rover Cam easier to locate in large spaces like a warehouse, that tower also projects a blue ring of light onto ceilings directly above the robot.

There’s no access to Alexa through the Rover Cam, which makes its included screen feel unnecessary. Instead of displaying a cute pair of eyes to encourage engagement, the Rover Cam’s screen is used to display status messages, including when it’s actively recording. It still has a microphone and speakers, but now they’re used for two-way talk functionality. Battery life is estimated to be about 30 minutes, allowing the robot to cover facilities around 5,000 square feet, but it’s limited to a single floor. For multiple levels, multiple robots would be needed, or the Rover Cam can be paired with Amazon’s new flying Ring Drone Cam.

This isn’t the first time that Amazon has attempted to repurpose Astro as a security robot. In 2023, it launched the $2,349.99 Astro for Business but discontinued it just a year later. The Ring Rover Cam is now available for preorder for $999.99 and is expected to ship starting on December 16th.

#249. The race is on to sue Nvidia

Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.

Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.

“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered.

Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.

The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.”

All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial.

While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.

From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.

The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument.

Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.

That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.

Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.

A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)

There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.

It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Adobe is expanding its Creative Cloud apps and Firefly AI platform with new capabilities that aim to make design and editing projects faster and less complicated. Some of the announcements from Adobe’s Max event today include features for automatically removing objects, blemishes, and other unwanted distractions in Premiere, Photoshop, and Lightroom, alongside new generative AI tools and collaborative experiences across Adobe’s apps and Firefly suite.

In Premiere, Adobe is introducing a new Generative Remove tool in beta that lets you erase unwanted objects and distractions like boom mics and background clutter directly on the video editing timeline. Users can mask and track an object, click Remove, and then Premiere “fills the area with realistic detail” using generative AI, according to Adobe, while the rest of the footage surrounding the erased area remains untouched. We saw a similar capability called Project Frame Forward demonstrated in last year’s Sneaks showcase, which is what Adobe calls the experimental features it’s developing.

Premiere is also getting new sound editing tools that help to quickly clean up messy recordings and separate various audio sources — including dialogue, music, ambience, and sound effects — into individual tracks and elements. The Generative Media tool Adobe introduced earlier this year is now generally available, alongside the new Color Mode color editing experience that Adobe launched in beta in April.

Photoshop now has an updated Remove Tool, which is better at detecting and reconstructing surrounding elements associated with the objects it’s erasing, such as reflections, shadows, and footprints. Features that are new to Photoshop include Quick Compare, which gives you a before-and-after canvas split-screen slider to review changes and edits without jumping between layers, and Relight, which adds new light sources that you can position around the canvas to dynamically adjust the lighting of images, with support for customizing hue and brightness.

The blemish removal tool in Lightroom on mobile is now coming to the desktop version, allowing you to retouch skin in photographs with a single tap. Open Eyes is also coming to Lightroom in public beta, which fixes blinking mishaps by replacing closed eyes with “natural-looking” open eyed results by matching a reference photo of the subject from your image library.

Adobe’s Firefly AI creative suite is getting new tools for video and image editing, and Quick Actions — ready-to-use workflows that specialize in automating specific tasks, such as making video thumbnails and product ads — are now generally available. Some new beta experiences are also launching in Firefly, including the Firefly Design combined edifying space for illustration, image editing, animation, 3D, and print. There’s also Firefly Graph, which “helps creators build and iterate on custom, repeatable workflows,” according to Adobe, and looks rather like the Weave platform that Figma introduced last year. And in private beta, Adobe introduced a Firefly Builder tool that’s designed around prototyping websites and apps — which also shares some similarities with Figma Make.

We’ve called out the most interesting announcements from Adobe Max here, but it’s just a fraction of the updates being showcased at the event. You can find the full list of all the new AI and design features announced today on Adobe’s blog.

#247. A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal

Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA. We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

#246. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#243. Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse

Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information.

Security researcher Robert Wiggins at What Security exclusively told TechCrunch that he found a password inside the source code of Wyndham’s Android app, which granted access to an internal company database, hosted by tech company Salesforce.

Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member numbers. The database also stores customer login tokens (called JWTs) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords. The database also contained Wyndham files and documents.

According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members.

The researcher said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, and asked for TechCrunch’s help in alerting the company. Soon after TechCrunch made contact with Wyndham’s cybersecurity staff, the exposed credential was revoked, preventing any further access to the database.

“Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access,” the statement added, without providing any further details about the claim.

Wyndham’s spokesperson would not say, when asked, whether the company had the technical means, such as server logs, to determine if anyone had access to the customer database prior to Wiggins’ discovery.

TechCrunch also asked Wyndham whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed, or disclose the incident to U.S. regulators, such as filing a notice with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as public companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents. Wyndham would not say.

Wyndham’s spokesperson also would not say for how long the password was embedded in its customer app, or how Wyndham plans to ship a long-term fix for the app.

App and software developers generally avoid including passwords or credentials in publicly released software and apps — a process known as “hardcoding” — as anyone with a copy of the software can extract the password and use it to access its associated server or database. Given the simplicity with which credentials can be abused by anyone, many cases of hardcoded credentials are automatically scored with a maximum vulnerability severity rating.

For Wiggins, this is his second public discovery of hardcoded credentials in two weeks, after finding a near-identical vulnerability in Applebee’s app that exposed customer data. Wiggins relied on AI tools for both discoveries, which make it easier to identify simple security weaknesses, such as hardcoded credentials, by scouring thousands of lines of decompiled app code every second.

When asked about Wyndham’s response, Wiggins told TechCrunch that he was glad the company fixed the issue, but noted that without visibility into any past activity, someone with malicious intent could have leaked large amounts of customers’ personal information.

The company would not say whether it planned to set up a vulnerability disclosure program to allow outside security researchers and hackers to privately report security vulnerabilities.

Michael Francess, Wyndham’s cybersecurity director who responded to the incident, told TechCrunch that researchers can alert [email protected] with details of potential security issues. The company’s spokesperson would not say whether it plans to change its website to allow researchers to alert the company.

This is the latest known security incident at Wyndham in recent years. In 2024, a security researcher found several Wyndham hotel check-in desks were running remote-access spyware that was leaking screenshots of guest records and booking information to the open web.

Soon after our reporting, the spyware app found on the hotel computers, called pcTattletale, was hacked and its banks of customer data stolen, forcing the company’s owner, Bryan Fleming, to shut down the company. Fleming, a former resident of Michigan, was later arrested by federal authorities and convicted of making, selling, and advertising unlawful spyware.

#241. Adobe is going all in on agentic AI

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Third-party AI agents can use Creative Cloud apps for you, and Firefly’s AI Assistant can run your social media accounts.

Third-party AI agents can use Creative Cloud apps for you, and Firefly’s AI Assistant can run your social media accounts.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Adobe is committing itself to the notion that chatbots and AI agents could be your next design assistant, or even automate creative workflows and repetitive tasks on your behalf. Some of the tools and features announced today at Adobe’s Max conference in Miami, Florida, include allowing your preferred third-party AI agents to access and change Creative Cloud projects, new capabilities for Adobe’s Firefly AI Assistant, and the ability for AI agents to keep perpetually running recurring work in the background.

Local Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations for Creative Cloud tools were previewed at the event, which aim to give you a choice between using Adobe’s own AI assistants, or the third-party agents you already use everyday. The integrations enable external AI agents from providers like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to work locally in Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects, where they can make direct changes to native project files on your computer.

You can take over from the agents at any time to manually refine the work because all layers, vectors, bins, and sequences remain editable. Agents that are connected to other MCP-capable tools can also include them in the same workflow, such as asking the AI agent to pull reference documents from Google Docs, design a project around them in Adobe’s tools, and then share the results with colleagues or clients in Slack. Creative Cloud local MCP integrations aren’t available yet, but Adobe says a private beta will be launching in early 2027.

“Always-on” agents were also previewed at Adobe’s Max event, which can perform recurring tasks continuously in the background, and allow you to focus on other work or step away from your computer entirely. You can assign them a job, such as organizing incoming assets, ongoing quality checks, or preparing content, and then review the agent’s plan and approve the final outcome. For example, an agent could be assigned to automatically turn all incoming images into promotional graphics for different social media channels, allowing you to check in daily and select the best results to publish. Adobe hasn’t specified when this preview will launch, but says it’ll be coming to Firefly AI Assistant first.

The Firefly AI Assistant beta, which is powered by Adobe’s creative agent, is also getting some upgrades. New capabilities include a Plan Mode that enables users to review, edit, and approve the agent’s plan before it starts running a task, a Model Selector that lets you specify which AI model to use for a project or leave it on auto-select to automatically assign the model based on the required results, and a new integration with Firefly Boards. Firefly AI Assistant now also lets you customize preferred formats, colors, brand guidelines, characters, and products, and choose to automatically apply those preferences across every project.

The creative agent has been used to stick AI assistants into Premiere, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io since it was introduced earlier this year, and now it’s expanding further into video editing. In Premiere, it can now be used to track masked subjects through a frame and apply effects or adjust color and exposure across entire clip sequences. The agent is also being added to Premiere mobile editing app, allowing you to make conversational video edits while on the go.

If it feels like Adobe is slapping agents and chatbots into all of its products then you’d be correct. That’s all according to the plan the company’s creativity head David Wadhwani laid out in April when he said the Adobe creative agent will eventually surface “in virtually everything we develop.” Whether it’s developing its own agentic solutions or throwing open the doors to third-party bots, AI agents will play a key role in Adobe’s future.

#240. Jensen Huang reportedly engaged a PR firm with a history of handling high-profile sex scandals a year ago

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang hired Heller Inc., a crisis communications firm known for handling sex scandals, at least a year before he publicly acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, Wired reported.

Heller Inc. founder Risa Heller has advised prominent men through personal scandals and sexual misconduct accusations, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her reported clients include former congressman Anthony Weiner, celebrity chef Mario Batali, and former New Yorker writer Jeffrey Toobin.

Wired also reported that Nvidia’s internal communications team was told to copy Heller Inc. on press inquiries about Huang shortly after an October 2025 New York Times report about whether Nvidia was helping Chinese companies evade U.S. chip export restrictions.

The Times reported that Megaspeed, a then little-known Singapore-based data center company with ties to China, had acquired nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. It described Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, the woman later linked to Jensen Huang, standing next to him at a Taipei gathering of Nvidia customers.

Heller and Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Sunday, Nvidia published a statement from Huang acknowledging an affair with a former Megaspeed executive, though he didn’t name Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board separately announced an independent investigation, citing reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

#238. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#237. Peak Design’s Roller Lite Carry-On is bigger on the inside — and cheaper, too

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

More efficient and more affordable, but less charming, too.﻿

More efficient and more affordable, but less charming, too.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When we sampled Peak Design’s Roller Pro last year, we loved almost everything about the camera gear powerhouse’s first attempt at a proper suitcase. Everything, that is, except for the price. Back then, during its crowdfunded launch, the Pro could be had for as little as $425. Today, you’re looking at $599.95 for the same roller bag.

Peak Design has taken that feedback to heart in creating the Roller Lite Carry-On, part of a new series of suitcases that bring many of the Pro’s features and design concepts into a hard-sided clamshell design that’s more traditional and, crucially, more affordable, starting with the $449.95 Lite Carry-On.

It’s part of a new Lite family of suitcases. The slightly larger Lite Carry-On Plus costs $469.99 and measures 22.5 x 15 x 9 inches, while the $549.95 Lite Trunk is 30 x 16.1 x 13.8 inches. The former should still squeeze in most overhead compartments, while the latter is better off checked. Both, though, come in cheaper than the Pro.

That cost-cutting does result in bags with fewer features and less originality, but I still found the new Lite Carry-On to be a great travel companion, first for a two-day whirlwind journey to Rome, then for a week in Tucson, Arizona.

I travel a lot, spending far more time escorting my carry-on around airports than I do driving my car at home, so no surprise that I’m picky about what I drag through terminals and haul up into overhead compartments. I wouldn’t say that aesthetics are a primary concern, but everybody prefers a good-looking suitcase, and the Roller Lite passes that first test. It’s understated yet sophisticated in black, but the emerald green option called cypress might be even better. There’s also a hue called stone for those more into earth tones.

Regardless of color, I think the Lite Carry-On’s hard plastic shell looks better than the soft-sided Roller Pro, and I’d hazard a guess it’ll stand the test of time better, too. The second trip I took with the Lite started in a tiny puddle-jumper of a plane. The flight attendant gate-checked any bag with wheels, even though the Lite Carry-On (21.7 x 13.8 x 9 inches, slightly smaller than the Pro) would have easily fit in the overhead.

It came back to me from its trip to the belly of the aircraft with a few new scuffs and scratches, otherwise looking only a little worse for wear.

Durability was a big selling point on the Roller Pro, and that continues here. The Lite is even more repairable thanks to its easily replaced strap handles. They sit flush without taking up any room in the suitcase itself, yet are quite comfortable to use.

Both the Pro and Lite share the same carbon fiber handle, also easily replaceable. It’s my favorite feature, rising smoothly and dropping into place without a hitch. I especially love the dry carbon weave that’s exposed when it’s raised.

My only complaint is that the handle on top is too bulky, making it a clumsy fit through the luggage passthrough on my backpack. But otherwise, the carbon construction makes for a sturdier feel than the handle on my Tumi 19 Degree Aluminum roller, which costs three times as much.

While both share the same handle, the Lite’s design is a substantial departure from the Pro. The Pro offered a so-called “hybrid” layout, with the top opening up and swinging back into a single large compartment. The Lite is a more traditional clamshell with a zipper running the full circumference, splitting the case in two like a book.

When it comes to packing camera equipment and other gear, I think the Pro’s single main compartment is easier to live with, especially if you’re hauling some bulky telephoto glass.

But when I’m packing more items of clothing than camera gear, I actually prefer the Lite Carry-On’s two smaller compartments. I can separate clothes from everything else, which is useful when living out of a suitcase.

The Lite Carry-On lacks the Pro’s trick external pockets for laptops, passports, and the like. That doesn’t bother me, as that stuff always goes in my backpack, but if you’re looking for a single-bag travel experience, the Pro is better suited. The Lite is also missing the Cord Hook feature of the Pro, potentially useful for strapping a tripod or the like to the outside.

Inside, the right half of the Lite has a zippered flap cover with two large mesh pockets that don’t look or feel as good as the inner pockets on the Pro. You’ll still find a hidden pocket for tucking away an Apple AirTag tracker, though.

The other side has the same elastic-strap holding system as the Pro. You load it up with stuff, then stretch the two hooks across to latch on the other side. It’s a basic, flimsy-looking solution, but it works. When the agents at Leonardo da Vinci International Airport wanted to rummage around in my bag, those little bungee hooks kept everything from scattering over the floor in Fiumicino.

The Lite Carry-On has an integrated, TSA-approved lock, something missing on the Pro, and though it’s slightly smaller on the outside (21.7 x 13.8 vs. 21.8 x 14), removing that front pocket makes it substantially bigger on the inside: 38 liters vs. 34 on the Pro, expanding to 45 liters vs. 39.

The 2-inch expansion on the Lite is a great emergency solution if you picked up a few too many souvenirs in Seville, but the Lite feels loose and floppy when rolling around with its expansion zipper open. I don’t recommend it.

Otherwise, when fully zipped and packed, I really enjoyed wheeling the Roller Lite around. It was an easy glider over smooth terminal floors and didn’t rattle obnoxiously over rougher asphalt.

The Roller Lite Carry-On is undoubtedly a simpler suitcase than the Roller Pro that preceded it, and because of that, it doesn’t feel nearly as special to use or purpose-driven as Peak Design’s offerings typically are.

But then it’s $150 cheaper, roomier, is easier to pack, and, in my estimation, will prove even more durable. It may not be the ultimate roller bag for pro photogs, but it’s my new favorite suitcase for under $500. I’d even put it ahead of options from Tumi, Briggs & Riley, and others that cost many times more, aren’t as easily repaired, and don’t come with a lifetime warranty.

#233. Aura’s next color E Ink photo frame is smaller, cheaper, sharper, and more colorful

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The new 10-inch version of the Aura Ink can display three new colors that help skin tones look more natural.﻿

The new 10-inch version of the Aura Ink can display three new colors that help skin tones look more natural.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Aura just launched a smaller version of its color E Ink frame with a handful of improvements and a more affordable price. The new Aura Ink frame features a 10-inch E Ink panel that can display more colors at a higher pixel density. It’s also differentiated from the original 13-inch model with a black frame and matching mat board that helps photos stand out.

The Aura Ink 10 is now available in the US for $349, $150 cheaper than the 13-inch version, which still costs $499. The original Ink’s price made it a tough sell over Aura’s other frames that are available with an LCD screen as large as 15 inches for $299. The new 10-inch option makes color E Ink more accessible, and it carries forward one of the Ink’s biggest advantages: a rechargeable battery so the frame can hang on a wall without a dangling power cord.

Although color E Ink displays have been available in e-readers like Kindles and Kobos for a few years, those devices use a color filter over a standard black-and-white e-paper panel with limited color reproduction. The Aura Ink instead uses E Ink’s Spectra 6 technology, which creates patterns of black, white, red, yellow, blue, and green ink droplets to reproduce a much wider color spectrum.

For the new 10-inch version, Aura worked with E Ink to add three custom base colors created by mixing those six inks in new ways: off-white, mustard yellow, and orange. The goal was to improve the company’s proprietary dithering algorithm to produce more natural-looking colors on faces, add detail to textures like grass, and to help smooth gradients so photos of sunsets, for example, look better. The 10-inch panel also has a higher pixel density — 200ppi, up from 150ppi on the 13-inch model — allowing it to produce slightly sharper results.

Both are welcome improvements, but in practice the color reproduction isn’t drastically better than the original. You’d need to compare the same photo on both models side by side to really see a difference, and the upgrades don’t overcome one of the major shortcomings of the Spectra 6 technology. While E Ink estimates it can reproduce around 65,000 different colors — and potentially even more with Aura’s enhancements — LCD displays can produce millions.

That can make it hard to predict how your photos will look on the new Aura Ink. Rich colors — like blue sky, green trees, and bright red flags — really pop, but skin tones can still sometimes look too warm or cold. I sent to the frame a photo of a bright-yellow water taxi photographed on a sunny day and expected it to appear well saturated, but that particular shade of yellow came out disappointingly subdued.

The technology still has its challenges, but the benefits of E Ink’s color displays make the new Aura Ink a tempting alternative to the company’s LCD-based frames, particularly for those who don’t want another glowing screen at home. Photos displayed on the Aura Ink look like a printed photo, even with a subtle front light that automatically adjusts to boost the lighting in a room.

It would fit right in on a wall of printed photos, and Aura estimates you’d need to take it down every three months to charge. But that’s if you update the displayed photo once every night. You can increase the frequency through Aura’s mobile app to up to 12 automatic refreshes per day, or manually change it using a set of buttons hidden on the back if you don’t mind charging the Ink more often. Just be mindful that unlike an e-reader that refreshes a page of text in less than a second, it takes the Ink about 30 seconds to change to a new image after a series of flickering, psychedelic patterns.

I’ve been testing it as a standalone picture frame using a removable support that props the Aura Ink up in landscape or horizontal orientations. Moving it around the house without hunting for an outlet first is a big plus. And as with all of Aura’s digital photo frames, the new 10-inch Ink also benefits from the polished mobile app that has helped make the company’s products so popular. You can send photos to the Ink through a Wi-Fi connection with free, unlimited cloud storage or create shared albums that friends and family can view and contribute to. It also works with Google Photos and Apple Photos. If you don’t have access to the app, you can text or email photos directly to the frame.

If you plan to gift an Aura frame during the holidays, the company’s LCD models are still more budget-friendly, with 10-inch options starting at $149. The new version of the Aura Ink still feels like a device for early adopters who completely understand the tradeoffs of E Ink’s color screens. But if you prefer the look of printed photos over a glowing LCD, the smaller Aura Ink is now one of the most affordable ways to try out this tech.

#232. Jensen Huang’s alleged honeypot scandal has inspired some top-notch memes

Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of the world’s most prominent chip company, has allegedly been honey-trapped by a suspected Chinese spy, and the news has struck the internet like a match to gasoline.

Huang has long been seen as a wife guy (or so everyone assumed). He and his wife, Lori, have been together since the 1980s, and both of their children work at Nvidia. Huang has been the closest thing the tech world has to a rock star, with fans lining up for selfies and autographs. Of all the AI overlords, the leather-jacket wearing Huang has seemed like the most level-headed and least erratic, which is why this plot twist has hit so hard.

The potential fallout is mind-boggling. Nvidia looms so large over the U.S. stock market that even the company’s domestic drama is a market risk. Countless AI startups depend on Nvidia chips, so any shake-up at the top would ripple far beyond the company. And Nvidia has no publicly disclosed succession plan, so if Huang leaves, it’s unclear who’d take over.

Is this how the AI bubble bursts? It’s a question that will be answered in time, but in the meantime, a more pressing matter demands our attention: ranking the funniest memes about the scandal, with bonus points for AI images presumably generated using Nvidia chips.

There’s admittedly a lot to choose from, ranging from “500 Days of Summer” jokes to jokes about divorce lawyers to an AI-adaptation of the music video for Usher‘s song “Confessions Pt. II,” a track about cheating. Another person created a viral AI video that recreates the Coldplay concert where a startup CEO was caught on the Jumbotron hugging a colleague.

Huang publicly confessed to the affair just yesterday, so the internet has the rest of the week to get creative.

#226. California’s proposed ‘billionaire tax’ fails to pass

California voters have rejected Proposition 40, the state’s proposed one-time tax on billionaires, the Associated Press reported Monday. The measure failed after an expensive campaign that pitted labor unions against some of tech’s wealthiest figures. It was also opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Nic Carter lives about as far from Silicon Valley as you can get within the continental U.S. but his feelings about California’s proposed tax on billionaires couldn’t have been stronger.

Carter, a Floridian, and a general partner at the crypto-focused venture capital firm Castle Island Ventures, told TechCrunch before the vote that he thought the proposal — it was on the ballot during California’s midterm election last week — would actually have been a huge win for more fiscally conservative states like his own.

“I think it’d be it would be great for Florida and Texas if these kinds of taxes pass,” Carter said last week. “I think it’s a shame, frankly, that California has this sort of semi-monopoly on capital formation, and that it’s being squandered by local governance that’s super dysfunctional.”

Proposition 40, otherwise known as the California “billionaire’s tax,” was a ballot measure that proposed the creation of a special one-time 5% wealth tax to be levied against state residents with a net worth of more than $1 billion. The tax, which would have been applied retroactively to anyone who was residing in California on January 1, 2026, would have been used to fund a number of public programs — most notably Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program that provides healthcare to qualifying low-income residents.

Proponents of the proposal — largely labor unions — said it would have inconvenienced a tiny number of state residents, as California has a little over 200 billionaires who own a cumulative total of approximately $2 trillion in wealth. In return, they said, it would generate massive amounts of revenue. Its backers projected it could have raised as much as $100 billion over five years, the likes of which could then have been used to support public healthcare and education.

But opponents argued that it would scare California’s wealthiest residents out of the state and ultimately disincentivize growth. The capital flight argument — that California’s upper crust would permanently flee, thus draining a more consistent source of revenue for the state — dominated conversations online among business leaders in the run-up to the vote. A critical but contested analysis published before the vote claimed the proposal would actually have lost the state money over time.

“You’re signaling to the entrepreneur class that you consider them a resource to be plundered,” he said.

Carter, who frequently works in San Francisco with tech startups, claimed such a tax would “inhibit venture capital investment” because VCs “wouldn’t necessarily want to invest in a company if they knew the founder was going to have to liquidate a huge percentage of their shares.” The logic: since many billionaires keep a majority of their wealth tied to their companies, it would be inconvenient for newly minted billionaires to make liquid a certain percentage of that wealth just so that they could pay the tax.

Jesse Tinsely, a California entrepreneur who has spent his life working in startups, agreed. Tinsely is the co-founder and CEO of Mainstreet, a fintech holding company that owns employment sites like Employer.com and Recruiter.com. Tinsely founded his first startup many years ago and said that, based on his own experience, what he had accomplished wouldn’t have been possible with the proposed tax. Additionally, he reiterated a widely held fear — that founders, who could be taxed on their corporate assets, would be incentivized to give up control over their companies.

“I bootstrapped my business. I have super voting shares, and I came from a [background as a] college dropout [and] broke firefighter with bad credit and whatnot, and built a business that’s valued into the billions,” Tinsely said last week. “I think it [the tax] removes the ability to do something like that.”

Tinsely said he felt the proposed tax “forces founders to opt into a system” where “anyone who wants to become an entrepreneur has to…raise money or some type of capital, or move. Those are basically the only two options.”

One of the key architects of the tax policy, Emmanuel Saez, told TechCrunch before the vote that fears about loss of founder control were unfounded, and not part of the design of the proposal. Saez, a French economics professor at the UC Berkeley, helped to create and promote the ballot measure alongside Gabriel Zucman, another Berkeley economist.

“The wealth tax hits you by diluting your economic ownership but [shares] can be easily structured to avoid losing any control rights,” Saez said, pointing to the fact that many billionaires only own a small percent of their companies. He’s also argued that stock can be structured to divorce economic ownership and voting control. Indeed, a common strategy to achieve this is called a dual-class share structure, which gives founders powerful voting rights even with limited shares.

Saez noted that AI has helped to drive a huge explosion in wealth in California but that much of that wealth is tied to a very small number of companies and individuals, many of whom won’t pay much back into the state’s coffers. He pointed out that California doesn’t really generate that much revenue from the billionaire class anyway. The state is estimated to take in about $3 billion a year from this group, representing about 1% of the total amount of revenue brought in between 2025 and 2026.

Despite its populist appeal, Proposition 40 struggled to win over enough Californians and was ultimately rejected. Invariably, many will cite voters’ lack of enthusiasm on a massive influx of spending that the bill’s opponents leveraged. The spending included as much as $379 million from the coffers of billionaires like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who funneled their money into a multi-pronged media assault designed to discredit it. The AP reported that the “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side.

Supporters of the measure signaled the fight isn’t over, though. The AP reported that backers said they could put a similar tax back on the ballot in 2028.

#224. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#222. Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages

Otter.ai, the AI-powered note-taking tool, announced Tuesday that it’s expanding its multilingual capabilities, including a new multilingual transcription feature that can follow conversations as speakers switch between languages during the same meeting.

The company is also adding support for 27 languages, its largest language expansion to date. Once the rollout is complete, Otter will support 31 languages in total, making the platform more accessible to international teams.

The upcoming feature will automatically detect language changes and continue transcribing without requiring users to adjust settings. For example, a call could move from English to Korean to Portuguese, with Otter following the conversation throughout.

The update aims to address a common challenge for global teams, where language differences can make meetings and collaboration more difficult.

“Otter is breaking down language barriers so any company, no matter where they’re based, can build a system of record for the decisions for voice AI communication,” an Otter spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Thirteen of the new languages are available now: Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, Italian, Cantonese, Portuguese, Russian, Indonesian, Malay, Dutch, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Polish.

The remaining 14 languages are coming soon and include Swedish, Danish, Finnish, Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Hebrew, Norwegian, Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Czech, Hungarian, and Romanian.

The newly added languages run on Otter’s own speech models. The company told us it trained them using publicly available datasets and worked with native-speaking volunteers to review transcripts and check accuracy.

The announcement comes as Otter continues to expand beyond transcription and into other workplace AI tools, following its $320 million funding from General Catalyst.

It recently introduced Work Mode, which uses meeting history and connected apps to help users prepare for upcoming calls. For instance, the feature pulls information from previous customer conversations, outstanding action items, notes from teammates’ similar calls, and recent Google Drive files.

Another recent addition is Live Assist, which provides real-time coaching during meetings. It analyzes the conversation and offers relevant suggestions based on what has already been talked about and what is happening in the moment.
