#220. Tech’s biggest names sunk a tax on billionaires’ wealth with $425m and a familiar playbook

California saw the most expensive opposition campaign in its history as funding of political campaigns broke records in the US midterms

In the hours after polls closed on election day, tech industry players began praising Sergey Brin, the co-founder of Google, on social media.

“Huge thanks to Sergey Brin here,” wrote Garry Tan, the CEO of Y Combinator. Venture capitalist Ilya Sukhar posted: “God bless Sergey Brin.” And David Marcus, a crypto entrepreneur, simply wrote: “Hero.”

They were all referring to Brin’s instrumental role in the defeat of California’s wealth tax ballot measure, known as Proposition 40. The proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state is poised to be defeated by double-digit numbers. Simultaneously, an opposition initiative that would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth, Proposition 42, put on the ballot by Brin and a cohort of the state’s ultra-rich, passed.

Brin, whose net worth is about $230bn, contributed at least $132m to the fight – more than any other donor. The runner-up was former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, who gave more than $48m. Millions more were donated by executives from Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with prominent venture capitalists. All told, Silicon Valley’s elite raised nearly $425m to sink the tax, according to campaign finance filings, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history.

Over the last month, the campaign poured those dollars into highly produced ads and mailers that bombarded voters with warnings that the tax was dangerous and would hurt everyday people. Taglines from the campaign said Prop 40 was an “everyone tax”, “reckless experiment” and “you’re next”. While supporters of the tax said the money would go toward funding the state’s healthcare losses from Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents repeatedly sent the message to voters that it would make healthcare funding worse.

Even without Prop 40’s outsized opponents, the pro-billionaire tax campaign had a difficult task. It had to convince Californians that this specific one-time tax, chiefly geared toward healthcare funding, was the right way to address losses from Trump’s bill. The idea of zeroing in on billionaires ruffled feathers across the state with major political figures opposing it, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, and Xavier Becerra, the governor elect.

Then there was the funding. In comparison with the billionaires’ war chest, the pro-Prop 40 camp, sponsored by the union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), raised just more than $31m. They were outspent nearly 14-fold.

“All lies have a shelf life,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW. “Billionaire-funded propaganda may mislead voters about the consequences of these cuts today, but as hospitals reduce services, emergency rooms close and families lose access to care, the truth will become increasingly difficult to hide.”

The counties that voted to pass Prop 40 are typically more Democratic and where many of the state’s wealthy reside, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and other areas around the Bay Area. The counties that overwhelmingly voted against the measure were mostly red, rural and poor. While many of these counties swung blue in US House races this election, up to 80% of voters there voted no on Prop 40, according to the latest count.

Rob Lalka, a business professor at Tulane University and author of The Venture Alchemists: How Big Tech Turned Profits Into Power, compared the Prop 40 campaign with Uber and Lyft’s ballot measure crusade in 2020, where the companies spent more than $200m to defeat an initiative over labor rights for drivers. The ride-hailing companies used similar tactics, Lalka said, something he describes as “misleading propaganda and paying for endorsements”.

“The money also seemed astonishing at the time: the amount to influence the outcome, over $200m, was a massive sum,” Lalka said. “Money in politics has only increased in California throughout this decade. That’s the context for Prop 40 this election cycle.”

The colossal funding of political campaigns has broken records nationwide this midterm cycle, said Francesco Trebbi, a business and public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He pointed to Elon Musk dumping $446m into House and Senate races across the county, but noted that it was ineffective in places such as Texas: Musk’s mark, James Talarico, won.

“Maybe it was easier to decouple Prop 40 opposition from President Trump’s agenda, so Brin had an easier target to hit,” Trebbi said. Still, he added: “We need a lot more data and statistical evidence in order to conclusively finalize this discussion.”

Exit polls haven’t yet been released for Prop 40, which will give more details on voters’ decisions. In the meantime, the SEIU-UHW’s Jimenez said that despite the loss, the union and its allies are not going to give up on the long game: “If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax.”

#217. Cyberattacks threaten to make open-source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns

The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast.

The October attack on OpenCode, which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.

The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers.

“The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.”

“You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute…but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation.

That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also make them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman.

“The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”

Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models, including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises and startups are relying on open models to build.

So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before.

For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it.

“Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.”

In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time.

Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related tradeoffs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open-source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid.

Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation.

“It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open-source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach.

The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.”

#215. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#214. US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped

New data comes after Republicans’ midterms losses – which were largely seen as a rebuke of the party over high prices

US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

Higher energy costs driven by the Iran war have been the main factor behind increased inflation, which has been above an annualized 3% since the war started in late February. In May, inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high, before fluctuating between 3.4% and 3.7%.

Energy prices continued to rise slightly in October, though increases were not as high as they were in September. In September, the monthly change in CPI from August was 0.6%.

The new data comes after a midterm election that will give Democrats control of Congress, in what was largely seen as a rebuke of Republicans over high prices. In their postmortem of the midterms, Republicans, including JD Vance, have specifically pointed to frustration over increased gas prices as a reason why the party fared so poorly in the election.

Gas prices cooled slightly in October, dropping from an average of $4.41 a gallon at the beginning of the month to $4.22 a gallon, prices are still more than $1 a gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA. On Monday, the average price for a gallon at the pump fell below $4 for the first time since July.

The cost of diesel, which is used to power trucks, farming equipment, buses and trains, is nearly $2.50 a gallon higher compared with prices last year but has also been going down since October. Gas prices have continued to drop.

In September, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and are expected to hike rates again at their next meeting in December. Higher interest rates slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive, and can slow inflation. The Fed’s target inflation rate is 2%, which it considers a stable pace for price increases.

Growth in the labor market surpassed economists’ expectations in October, giving more room for the Fed to hike rates. The unemployment rate has been relatively steady, hovering just above 4%.

Because today’s inflation is so closely tied to energy prices, it’s unclear how much and how quickly a rate hike could ease prices. But the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank is dedicated to making sure price increases ease up.

“Our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” Warsh said on 28 October.

Consumer sentiment increased slightly at the end of October as gas prices eased, according to the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers. At the same time, the US stock market was experiencing a dip as investors voiced skepticism over the influx of AI spending.

“While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of ​a relatively ​turbulent period ⁠in stock markets,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, in a statement. “Moreover, ​consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over ​a ⁠possible AI bubble.”

#212. Ring, known for its doorbell cameras, launches a home security drone and an enterprise security robot

Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is launching its own robotics division, with an eye toward automating security at both the home and the office. The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy.

The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out. The other item that the company is launching is a roving enterprise security robot, designed for businesses.

First, the drone. Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work. Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them. It has been built to integrate with Ring’s other home security devices so, for instance, if a Ring alarm goes off in a particular part of the home (say, the backdoor), the bot will supposedly fly to that location and investigate. When it’s not in use, the drone stays inactive in a docking bay.

The drone shoots video in 2K and it also comes equipped with LED lights so that it can keep watch at night and record video in low light. It can be controlled via Amazon’s Alexa Home Map, and the bot can also be scheduled to patrol the house at specific times — so, if you know you’re going to be out for the night or even on vacation, the drone can keep you apprised of what’s happening while you’re away.

Now, let’s turn to Ring Rover Cam. Like the drone, this roving robot can be set to patrol specific routes, at specific times, within the user’s business. The robot streams video in continuous 4K, which is viewable via Ring’s mobile app, and a trigger can be set to automatically record if it detects a human. It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot.

Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot. The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says.

“Together, it’s like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out,” the company claims, of its new devices. “Ring Rover can do a sweep of the floor after close and investigate when sensor trips at 2 a.m. — streaming it all to your phone, wherever you are.”

Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture.

The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270.

#209. Spotify’s AI DJ gets new voices, personalities, and an option for less chatter

Spotify’s AI DJ, one of the company’s earlier efforts in embracing AI technology to connect people with their favorite music, is getting an upgrade. On Tuesday, the streamer announced that users will now be able to customize their DJ more like they can an AI assistant, by choosing between different voices and personalities. Those who like the feature, but not all the chatter, can also now opt for an experience with less commentary in between sets.

Since first launching the AI DJ in 2023, Spotify has leveraged AI across to improve all areas of its app. Most recently, that has included updates that allow users to chat with a conversational AI agent about music, fine-tune their recommendations with prompts, create playlists with AI, and work with third-party agents like ChatGPT and Claude. However, the DJ remains one of Spotify’s most popular AI features, as it’s used by over 94M Spotify Premium listeners.

Now, it’s revisiting one of its first major AI features, taking a cue from the personalization options other AI assistants routinely offer.

The different voices will have their own unique personalities as well. For instance, users can pick between three American voices, one of which is laid-back and warm (Casey), another that’s direct and has an edge (Tess), and a third that has a Southern accent and a youthful energy (Lane). In addition to the other various regional accents, there are also two new Spanish voices, one that’s more down-to-earth (Nico) and one that’s more witty and friendly (Fabi).

The voices will not replace the AI DJ’s original voice, “X,” which was based on that of a Spotify employee’s real voice recordings. However, DJ Fabi and Nico will now be the only Spanish voices available, replacing the earlier “Livi.”

The other change allows users to toggle off the commentary between songs, reducing the DJ’s interruptions. While typically, the AI DJ introduces different selections of music, explaining what it picked and why, users can now limit it to brief acknowledgements when they first start the DJ feature and when they turn it off. Spotify says this would allow people to use the DJ at times they may have turned to a playlist instead, like when hosting a party where they want music in the background, but not the chatter.

To access the DJ, users can search for the term “DJ” in the search bar of the Spotify app on their device, then tap the three-dot menu to pick their voice and commentary settings. To change genres, artists, or recommendations while the DJ is driving things, you simply tap the DJ button again.

Spotify says the new voices begin rolling out today, November 10, to Premium users in the markets where DJ is already supported. Currently, that includes over 95 global markets, where the DJ is supported in English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

#207. Historic ocean liner to ‘live on’ beneath waves as world’s biggest artificial reef

The SS United States will sink off Florida coast to become an artificial reef, ending long-running wrangle over its fate

Final preparations were under way on Tuesday to sink the world’s fastest ocean liner in the Gulf of Mexico as an artificial reef, concluding a decades-long wrangle over the fate of the transatlantic icon.

A fleet of five tugboats moved the rusting hulk of the SS United States from a quayside in Mobile, Alabama, on Monday for its short journey to 25 miles off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be scuttled in a precision operation on Wednesday afternoon.

The vessel’s subdued final journey was a far cry from its flagship heyday more than half a century ago when presidents, royalty and celebrities were among passengers surrounded by opulence on their travels to and from Europe.

It will sink stripped of its two giant funnels and mast, and barely recognizable from the one-time crown jewel of the cruise industry that still holds the blue riband for the fastest transatlantic crossing by a passenger liner. Its July 1952 eastbound journey of three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes at an average of almost 36 knots (41.4mph) has never been surpassed.

Becoming an attraction for divers as the world’s largest artificial reef was not the ending preservationists had sought for the ship, which was withdrawn from service by the now defunct United States Lines in 1969 amid declining passenger numbers and the growth of transatlantic air travel.

At various times it was intended to become a floating hotel, a museum, or a hospitality venue, but none of the proposals raised enough money or momentum to come to fruition.

It languished at docksides in Virginia and Pennsylvania as those plans stalled, a protracted legal fight over its future played out, and the liner passed through several owners, including the SS United States Preservation Society, a non-profit founded in 1992 to save it from being scrapped.

In 2021, port authorities in Philadelphia doubled the daily dockage fees to $1,700, an amount the conservancy said it could not afford, and the fast-deteriorating vessel was eventually evicted by court order in 2024.

It was destined to be broken up until Florida’s Okaloosa county stepped in to purchase it for $1m later that year, and advanced the reef project that comes to fruition this week. Months of preparation work followed the ship’s relocation to Mobile, including removing internal fixtures and toxic materials, and it will be sunk by controlled flooding, meaning no explosives will be used.

Divers will be able to visit the 990ft (300-meter) ship on the seabed, a depth of about 180ft, from this weekend.

Susan Gibbs, the conservancy’s president and co-founder, said the group was appreciative that even though it will be out of public view, people could still enjoy visiting the SS United States, and hearing about its story.

Plans are advanced for a shore-based museum, featuring the funnels and items from the ship, and a pier from which diving trips to the reef will depart.

“While she will soon rest beneath the waves, her story will live on,” said Gibbs, who is the granddaughter of William Francis Gibbs, designer of the SS United States and one of the most celebrated and prolific maritime architects of the 20th century.

“That’s why the museum is such an inspiring and important component of all of this. The conservancy, over the past 20 years has collected an amazing array of artifacts and material from the ship, and film, and testimonials of those who sailed on her, and worked on board.

“She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat, so that, combined with the land-based museum and visitor experience, will honor her history in a deeply moving way.”

Her grandfather, Gibbs said, would be touched that so many people worked hard to preserve what he always considered among his finest accomplishments, a record-breaking ocean liner built entirely in the US that exemplified what he saw as the best of American industry and ingenuity.

“He died when I was five, but I came to know him well through the ship, and through the letters and speeches and papers that I have spent a lot of time perusing,” she said.

“His relationship with the ship was, I would say, a full bore obsession. He would joke that he loved the SS United States a thousand times more than my grandmother. He would see the ship off every time she set sail for Europe, and be one of the first to greet her on her return.

“He had a true love affair with the ship.”

#205. After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to StatCounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. He is rather targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies including Perplexity and OpenAI were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

#204. Pete Hegseth dismisses Republican’s impeachment effort against him as ‘a political spectacle’ – US politics live

Trump’s defense secretary calls impeachment effort from congressman Thomas Massie ‘a personal manifesto driven by ego’ as he faces scrutiny for prolonged Iran war

Pete Hegseth has started his Pentagon press conference.

He took the podium and immediately blasted Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against him, that the outgoing Republican introduced on Monday.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability,” Hegseth said.

“It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”

As of now, the president has no events open to the press on his schedule. While he’ll spend most of the day in closed-door meetings, he’ll take part in signing time at 3.30pm ET, and we’ll let you know if that opens up to reporters.

Following Pete Hegseth’s press conference, Donald Trump issued a brief, and glowing, assessment of his defense secretary’s performance, while blasting the Republican representative who is moving to impeach him.

“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” the president wrote on Truth Social.

One quick note – since Thomas Massie introduced his articles of impeachment on Monday, the House now has until Wednesday to take them up.

The lower chamber can hold a vote on the House floor, decide to send the resolution to committee (for further investigation) or table the measure entirely.

A vote could come as soon as today. We’ll keep you updated.

After several Republicans, including vice-president JD Vance, said that the party’s shellacking in the midterm elections was due to the ongoing Iran war and spike in prices as a result of the conflict, Hegseth danced around whether he agreed.

“I respect the vice-president greatly, and I’m certainly not going to exchange in any finger pointing. And thankfully, politics is not really my thing,” the defense secretary said. “But I agree with what the president said when he said: ‘hey, if if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.”

Hegseth referred back to secretary of state Marco Rubio’s sentiment that the war, now in its eighth month, is “not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary”.

“That’s certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking,” Hegseth added.

A point that Hegseth has repeated throughout his briefing is that Thomas Massie’s resolution is merely a “policy disagreement” that defense secretary said should be solved by legislation and debate.

Hegseth also used his time today to disparage the media for ignoring military successes. “You hate the president more than you love our country, or our troops,” he told reporters at the Pentagon.

During his press conference, Hegseth was resolute that the articles of impeachment are baseless, and that all attacks were carried out legally.

“As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen, everyone was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs,” he said. “We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s the job well done.”

So far, Hegseth has simply dismissed many of Massie’s impeachment articles, running through – what he describes – as a series of defense successes.

Hegseth, instead, deemed the effort to remove him from office as an act of “sabotage”.

“It tells them that a single rogue legislator, loaded with personal animus for the president, can attempt to veto national security decisions made by the duly elected commander-in-chief. It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time,” Hegseth said.

In his opening remarks, Hegseth yoked himself to Donald Trump, who was impeached twice in 2019 and 2021 – during his first term.

“We’ve seen this show before. They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call. They impeached him again in his final week in office. Both times they failed,” Hegseth said.

“Now they’re trying a third time. This time against a member of his cabinet. They will fail again. And if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”

Hegseth noted that it has been 150 years since the last defense secretary was impeached. That was William Belknap in 1876, who served under President Ulysses S Grant. Belknap was eventually acquitted by the Senate.

The US military said it was taking “coordinated and appropriate” security steps after flight-tracking data showed it had withdrawn at least a dozen aircraft from a second British airbase.

The removal on Monday of the American refuelling tankers and other aircraft from Mildenhall Royal Air Force (RAF) base in eastern England followed a threat from Iran, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.

Citing people familiar with events, the newspaper said the “precise nature” of the Iranian threat remained “under discussion” among United States officials, AFP reported.

During a White House press conference, Trump said Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and an escalation was not needed:

The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).

The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.

Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.

Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by president Donald Trump, signalling demand for quick action to address ⁠the high cost of living, ⁠a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The ​four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans – including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans – want US Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside US ally Israel in ⁠February.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 in last week’s midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump’s Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war. Democrats will take power when the new Congress ⁠is sworn in on 3 January.

On their first day back in the Capitol after comprehensive defeats in last week’s midterm elections, Republicans were divided into two camps: those who saw the catastrophe coming, and those who did not.

“I told you exactly what was going to happen. Over and over and over, I told you,” said West Virginia senator Jim Justice. “I said really and truly, if you weren’t concerned and you were a Republican, you were living in a cave. That was my exact words.”

“No one anticipated the magnitude,” said congressman Warren Davidson of Ohio. “I mean, you can’t tell me that the guy that ran as a Democrat for senator in Mississippi thought he was going to win.”

While Scott Colom hasn’t officially been declared the winner in Mississippi’s knife-edge US Senate race – a state that has not sent a Democratic to the chamber since 1982 – there was indeed plenty of evidence before the Tuesday vote that Republicans were in for it.

Not only does the party in power historically suffer defeats in midterm elections, but Donald Trump’s approval ratings had cratered with voters, even on issues that he had previously polled well on, while Democrats had surged in both special and off-year elections.

Nonetheless, few pollsters or political analysts were publicly forecasting the 54-seat Senate majority and 254-seat House majority Democrats won – both of which may expand even further as ballot counting continues.

“People are mad, and they have a right to be mad. They’re disappointed, and they feel like we haven’t delivered, and we deserve exactly what we got,” said Senator John Curtis of Utah. His state is deeply red, but last Tuesday Democrats managed to break the Republican supermajority in the state house of representatives by gaining at least 14 seats – a feat repeated in legislatures across the country.

Under pressure after President Donald Trump and Vice-president JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican party’s sweeping losses in midterm elections, Hegseth now faces impeachment proceedings in the House of Representatives.

#202. Aura’s newest e-ink photo frame is even better and more affordable than its last

If you’re into interior design, decorating, or just love displaying your family photos, Aura‘s latest product line will feel magical. Aura’s cordless Ink photo frames have the versatility of a digital photo frame, but their e-ink displays don’t even look digital, blending seamlessly into the rest of your framed photos.

A follow-up to its 13-inch, $499 Ink frame, Aura is unveiling a new product that’s a little less pricey: a 10-inch Ink frame that is now on sale for $349.

“Ten years ago when we were first starting Aura, we were interested in making an e-ink picture frame. We just wanted a frame that looked like a printed photo and magically changed, but the tech was not there at that point,” Aura co-founder and CTO Eric Jensen told TechCrunch. “So it’s great to be able to see it moving forward.”

Aura uses E Ink’s Spectra 6 display for its Ink frames, which can only render six different colors. What sets Aura apart is its proprietary dithering algorithm, a technique that blends a limited color palette into patterns that the eye reads as smooth gradients.

While the 13″ Ink frame looks beautiful, it is obvious that the colors are not exact to the original photo. For the new 10″ Ink frame, Aura worked with E Ink on expanding its Spectra 6 technology to incorporate three new proprietary colors: off white, mustard, and orange.

“The net effect is that the edges are smoothed a bit more,” Jensen said. “You can see if you zoom in on a face, the places where we would’ve had to previously put white next to red, or something a little more jarring, we can now fill in with the right color, and it effectively makes it a little bit higher resolution.”

With the extra three colors, the Ink 10″ is getting truer to representing an original photo, but the colors still appear less saturated on the digital display than in a printed image.

For both Ink frames, Aura paid special attention to rendering skin tones accurately, since most people use these frames for family photos. (Personally, I think the slight variations in color give scenery photos a cool, vintage look). It may not matter as much if your kid’s bright pink shirt looks closer to red on the Ink, but if her skin is unnaturally grey, then it would look pretty weird, hence Aura’s meticulous calibration of these colors.

The 10″ frame only comes in one colorway: a black frame with a dark grey linen-textured mat. It looks a bit jarring at first, and I wouldn’t hang it on a gallery wall next to ten other white-matted photos, but it looks great on its own.

“We intentionally made it dark so that it didn’t have as much contrast with the e-ink display next to it,” Jensen said.

Like Aura’s other frames, the Ink 10″ is compatible with Aura’s app, where customers and their family and friends can easily upload photos from their phone to an album of photos that display on their frame.

“On average, there’s about four people sharing to each frame,” Jensen said, meaning that it’s common for customers to share their Aura albums with others. If your mother has an Aura frame, for example, she can grant you permission to add photos to her frame, letting you easily drop the newest photos of her grandson at the park.

On Ink frames, the company recommends setting the frame to only update once per day, since changing photos consumes battery life (and it’s a bit odd to watch the dithering algorithm in action).

Aura comes with hanging hardware, a stand, and a USB-C charging cable, and the company claims that the Ink 10″ can last three months on a single charge. In my experience with the Ink 13″, I’d say the battery actually lasts about a month. But this is perhaps because I had displayed it in an area of my home that gets a lot of light, so the front light is probably lit more often than if I had placed it elsewhere.

The new Ink frame still doesn’t generate perfect, one-to-one reproductions of your photos, but the precision of color doesn’t matter that much. What matters more is that, if you aren’t expecting it, you could easily be fooled into thinking that the Ink 10″ is just an ordinary framed photo.

#201. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#198. Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion

Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.

The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.

The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise, but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.

Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.

All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion to $93.7 billion.

Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.

As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.

Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC, under the ticker symbol “ANT”.

Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue came in at $17 billion, and nine-month revenue was $33.2 billion. The company reported a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments hitting $900.9 billion. It has nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments.

OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after it raised $11 billion, nearly half the $20 billion it had first tried to raise.

#196. ‘It wasn’t long until he asked me if I’d ever had sex before’: David Walliams accused of preying on young women for sex

Comedian and former Britain’s Got Talent judge alleged to have groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15 and harassed women in the workplace over a number of years. He denies the allegations

Alex had just returned from school and was watching The Simpsons in her bedroom when the phone rang. She distinctly recalls the first thing he said. “Hi, it’s David Walliams. You know, off the telly!” It was January 2004. Alex was 15 and studying for her GCSEs. Walliams was 32 and a rising star with the comedy sketch show Little Britain.

A few days earlier, Alex had been to a fan event where Walliams had signed autographs as his character Lou. Wearing a frizzy wig and a black leather jacket, he looked up at Alex as her mother took a photograph. As she approached Walliams, Alex remembers him saying: “You’re a very attractive lady.”

With ambitions of becoming a comedy writer, Alex says she gave him some printouts of scripts she had written. She included a cover letter with her contact details, but she did not expect him to get in touch.

When he did, she was so excited that immediately after the call she made a record of the conversation in youthful scrawl across four sides of A4 paper. “David Walliams phoned me!!” she wrote. “He said he thought my scripts are VERY FUNNY!” She noted how Walliams had been surprised when she told him she was still at school, asking her: “Right, so you’re, what, 15, 16?”

The notes describe how they talked about her exams, as well as the enticing possibility of him getting tickets for her to watch a live performance of Little Britain. At the end of the call, he told her to stay in touch. He gave her his email address after she reassured him she would not pass it on to anyone. “He said that he trusts me,” she wrote.

Over the next two years, Alex says, she and Walliams spoke on the phone on a couple of occasions and exchanged multiple emails. She was amazed that a rising star of the comedy world was suggesting he could help her. By the time she was 17, she says, they were having sex.

Alex is one of multiple women who allege Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. Some, like Alex, say their interactions with Walliams were traumatising and have requested that pseudonyms be used to protect their anonymity.

Most say they were over 18 when they had interactions with Walliams. But a woman whom the Guardian is calling Jade alleges that, like Alex, she met him when she was 15. She says that weeks after he first made contact, he invited her to his house and initiated sexual contact.

The allegations extended to his conduct in the workplace, with several sources describing inappropriate behaviour towards women at both the prime-time show Britain’s Got Talent (BGT) and his publisher HarperCollins.

In September, HarperCollins announced it would no longer publish Walliams’ extensive back catalogue, having dropped its bestselling author last year. Few reasons were given for the seismic move. The Guardian and ITV News can now reveal that the publisher severed ties with the star author after concerns were raised about his behaviour over several years, including an allegation that he had inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee and pursued another.

Walliams denies any wrongdoing. Earlier this year his lawyers took a case to the high court to try to stop the allegations being published. The case was dismissed, so now the women’s stories can be revealed.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on this investigation, Walliams wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

“I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

A multimillionaire and OBE recipient, Walliams, 55, is one of the most famous comedians and writers in the UK. He built a career on his cheeky, flamboyant persona, which has permeated his children’s books, comedy work and the decade he spent as a much-loved judge on BGT.

Back in 2004, Walliams was at the beginning of his journey to success. His big break had been Little Britain, the provocative sketch show he created for BBC Radio 4 with his comedy partner, Matt Lucas. The show, which later moved to television, featured now infamous characters including the perma-tracksuited Vicky Pollard and the interdependent duo Lou and Andy. In December 2004, it won the top accolade at the British Comedy Awards.

At the awards ceremony, Walliams was captured on film dressed in a black dinner jacket, seemingly utterly relaxed and enjoying himself. He threw his head back in laughter as the compere, the TV chatshow host Jonathan Ross, opened the show with a joke pointedly referencing him: “The comedy awards is 15 years old – 15 years old! And like most 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams.”

Ross, responding through lawyers, said he did not write the joke himself.

Alex says she remembers watching the show from her bedroom. Walliams had been in touch several times since the first, unexpected call 11 months earlier. In February 2004, he had sent a postcard. On the front, Walliams had drawn a love heart across a photo of himself and Lucas dressed as Little Britain characters. On the back, he had written: “Thanks for your email. Stay in touch. It’s great to hear from you again. I hate typing so let’s speak. I’ve lost your number, please can you E-mail it to me?

They discussed the possibility of her doing work experience, which she says fell through. Walliams continued to encourage her writing, she says. “I was excited,” she remembers. “I can see that he was probably trying to make me feel special.”

Then Walliams’ interest appears to have cooled. Emails over a period of 19 months into 2005 give the impression of a schoolgirl desperate for support with her aspiring career. But Walliams rarely responded, and when he did, the replies were brief, even curt.

Alex says this left her feeling confused: “He was the one spending hours on the phone to me, like telling me and promising me that I could do all this stuff. And then he shut it down. Which was confusing for me because he had been so approachable and chatty before and I just didn’t want to let a connection go.”

Alex sent an email about a gig she was planning to go to in London and Walliams replied, late at night.

How are you? How old are you now? What are you up to? Are you still writing?

Alex, who by then was nearly 17 and a half, responded that she was “old enough to go drinking haha” and sent four closeup photos of her face. In two, she is smiling and looks relaxed. The others show her lying on her bed, staring flirtatiously into the camera. Walliams was 34.

How much school have you got left? Is this your final year?

well i dont go to school anymore i go to college… and yeah final year which is nice

Those pictures are really lovely by the way.

Alex obliged, sending pictures of her with classic 00s poker-straight hair and dark eyeliner.

Alex says that later that evening they spoke on the phone and that Walliams suggested meeting up for sex. She says: “The tone had massively become sexual.”

The next day, Walliams was interviewed on BBC Radio 1. The presenter Scott Mills brought up the comedian’s reputation as a womaniser and asked whether his friends worried about introducing their girlfriends to him. “What, I’m some sort of rabid animal?” Walliams replied. “No, I’m a gentleman, but no, I just, I love the company of women, you see.”

Over the following months, Alex says, she received calls and text messages from Walliams and he asked for more photographs. “At first, I just sent photos of my face,” she says. It progressed to photos of her in her underwear, she adds, then Walliams started “telling me how to pose”. One photo, sent in November 2005, shows the 17-year-old reflected in a mirror, provocatively pulling down the waistband of her black bikini. She says she took the photographs in her bedroom; in some she was naked.

“I hadn’t done that before,” Alex recalls. “I could really feel the imbalance at that point already, but equally I was young and there was an element of excitement, because of the context of who he was to me.”

Lawyers acting for Walliams say he understood her to be 18 when she got back in touch and that he does not recall, and does not believe, that he asked Alex to send him sexual pictures of herself. He does not deny that they met a few months later.

In spring 2006, Alex and Walliams were having sex.

Alex recalls going to Walliams’ flat in Belsize Park, north-west London, on three separate occasions. The first, she says, when she was 17.

She says she remembers being struck by his height as he let her in. At nearly 1.9 metres (6ft 2in), he seemed to fill the doorway. Soon after walking through, she recalls, “he just, like, shoved his tongue in my mouth”. She says sex quickly followed: “We went on his bed and yeah, we had sex.”

She says he did not use a condom. “I remember clocking it and feeling a bit like that’s not good but I was too young. I really didn’t, I really don’t think I would have had the ability to get the words out at that point to say ‘don’t do that’.”

On the second occasion they met, she says they had oral sex. She says all three encounters were consensual, but they were brief. On two of the instances they had sex, she says, he asked her to wait in a cafe and then called her to tell her to come.

Catchphrases from the show, which had drawn 10 million viewers for its third season, were being repeated across the country. In his autobiography, Walliams wrote about this period: “I became so well known that when I walked down the street every second person recognised me. Women threw themselves at me. And sometimes I caught them. Then I became rich.”

In July that year, Walliams was feted in the press for his 21-mile (34km) charity swim across the Channel. At the Pride of Britain awards that November, he was voted Britain’s most inspiring public figure.

But Alex was starting to question what was happening. She says she tried to break things off by refusing to meet him. Walliams did not seem to get the message and she says he would periodically contact her to ask for sex. Once, when she was 18, she says he drove up to a pub she was drinking in and begged her to come to his house for sex. When she refused, she says he suggested she give him oral sex in his Aston Martin instead. Again, she says, she refused.

Alex spoke about her experiences across several interviews over more than a year. Looking back, she is clear about what she feels happened. “I think I was groomed, 100%. We met when I was 15 and he was promising to help me and was a figure of authority and someone that I looked to for guidance and help. He used that power and abused that power the minute he felt he just about could and it was just about safe to.”

Walliams’ lawyers say the suggestion he groomed Alex is false and has caused him significant distress. They add that Walliams wrote to Alex when she was 15 to encourage her writing and that Walliams always tried to engage with fans, whatever age or gender, as he appreciated that such encouragement would mean a lot to them.

The lawyers say it was Alex who got back in touch with him later, and that Walliams believed she was 18 at this point. They say she did not raise, and he did not believe, that she had any concerns about the sex at the time. They say he believes he used a condom, as he did with any new partner. They add that Walliams denies he was “pushy”.

They say it was Alex who contacted Walliams from outside the pub and that he does not believe he made any proposal that they have sex.

The lawyers add that Walliams was mortified to learn that their brief, consensual relationship had caused her sadness.

Alex still gets emotional when she recalls the experience. “I want to vomit. I hate him. My body reacts when I think about it. It’s like a trauma response,” she says.

“I never said no,” she says, “but I felt unable to say anything or have any control in that situation once I was with him.

“OK, it’s legal to have sex when you’re 17, 18 – 16, even,” she adds, “but the context of who you’re having sex with – if that person is double your age, if that person has known you from a young age and promised you things and is in a much bigger position of power than you, both in age, in work, in finance, in stature and size, like, everything, I really don’t think that’s OK.”

Like Alex, Lilly Creightmore was an avid comedy fan. In July 2003, she went with her mum to a filming of Little Britain. She remembers Walliams staring intently at her from the side of the stage.

She noticed him again when she went to see a show inside an Agent Provocateur store in London. Creightmore had been a model, appearing on the reality TV show Model Behaviour when she was 16.

Then a card arrived out of the blue. Sent to her mother’s house, it pictured a young girl, arms crossed, with feathered angel wings either side of her. It was from Walliams, asking her for a date. He wrote: “When I saw you in Agent Provocateur I so wanted to speak to you but amongst all those frilly knickers I couldn’t find the words.” She had no idea how Walliams had found her name or address.

Curious, Creightmore says she called the number he had provided in the card. She was 18. Walliams was 32. She agreed to meet him for dinner.

She says she explicitly told him she was interested only in friendship, but over the years she knew him he would constantly pester her for sex. Looking back, she feels he tried to coerce her into sleeping with him.

She had been trying to make it as a photographer and says Walliams offered to help, buying her books and offering to introduce her to artists she admired. He took her to celebrity-packed parties, where she remembers feeling awkwardly young and out of place. At one event she remembers, the guests included Jonathan Ross, Ricky Gervais and the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who says he does not remember the occasion.

After Creightmore fell out with her mother, Walliams invited her to stay with him for a couple of weeks at the end of 2003. She slept on the sofa but recalls that every night Walliams “would plead with me to share a bed with him and, you know, paw at me”, she says. “At some point, he put his head in my lap and made me stroke his head.” She adds: “I didn’t feel safe there and it wasn’t a good situation, so I had to go stay somewhere else.”

Ben (not his real name), a friend of Walliams’ at the time, recalls seeing Creightmore at a house party Walliams threw in the days she was there. It was Ben who had helped Walliams track down her contact details through the producers of the modelling show she appeared on when she was 16.

Against the backdrop of the lad culture of the early 00s, Ben had thought of Walliams as something of an “old-fashioned romantic” in his pursuit of women. He had a pattern, Ben says: “See a woman, think she’s attractive, find out how to contact her, send her flowers via that contact asking her out to dinner. Take her out for dinner, invite her back to yours. If she doesn’t come, be sad. Phone her every day until she agrees that the next time she will come.”

Now Ben is concerned that women may have felt uncomfortable with Walliams’ attention. He and Walliams fell out years ago, but he recalls that Walliams told him he (Walliams) was a sex addict. It is something the comedian wrote about in his autobiography when describing mental health issues in the early 00s. “I thought sex could take away my sadness,” Walliams wrote. “However, it just made it worse. And I sank lower and lower into despair. I had become a sex addict.”
