If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

To send a message to Maeve McClenaghan please choose the ‘UK Investigations’ team.

If you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email maeve.mcclenaghan@theguardian.com.

You can message Maeve using the Signal Messenger app. Use the ‘find by username’ option and type ‘maevemcclenaghan.45’.

Finally, our guide at theguardian.com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

Looking back, Creightmore now considers Walliams’ behaviour “highly inappropriate” and says she feels he abused his power. “He was pursuing me, you know, at a vulnerable age and place in my life, for sexual gratification,” she says.

“Yeah, I was a young adult, but I was a vulnerable young adult. [He was] making me feel special, plying me with gifts and then sort of disregarding me when he wasn’t getting what he wanted.”

Lawyers for Walliams say he denies grooming Creightmore or behaving inappropriately. They add that he did not target her because she was vulnerable or young, nor did he manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him. They say the gifts and offers to help her came with no expectations. Walliams, they say, has a passion for photography and he wanted to help her with this career.

They say he had understood their friendship, which lasted for about five years, to be special and that he was devastated by the account she had given to this investigation, which came as a complete surprise.

In summer 2007, Jade clicked on to MySpace. She was 15 and says her date of birth was on her profile page. There in her inbox was a direct message from Walliams.

Jade was not exactly a fan of Little Britain, but she knew who Walliams was. Rumours about his love life featured regularly in the tabloid newspapers that her dad would leave lying around the house. In 2007 alone, the comedian appeared in hundreds of articles, often accompanied by photographs of him with a woman he was rumoured to be dating.

Jade recalls how, after she had posted on a comment thread below a photograph of Walliams, the comedian had sent her the private message. “I ignored it,” she says. “Why would he want to talk to me?” But about 10 minutes later, she remembers, she received another message. This time, she says, she replied and Walliams asked for her phone number.

Although it was late when her phone rang, she recalls walking out into the garden so she would not be in earshot of her parents, who were sitting in the lounge. She remembers how she felt cold as she chatted to Walliams about school and what she wanted to do in the future.

Jade had had a tough few years and was struggling with her mental health. Her abiding memory of the call, she says, was how she felt special. “You get this celebrity approaching you – that’s a whole different level of attention,” she says. “Then you think: oh, I must be a bit special in a way.”

Walliams gave the 15-year-old his email address – the same address he had used to message Alex when she was 15. Jade says she and Walliams started to write to each other; sometimes she used her school email account.

Excited, Jade says, she showed her two best friends the MySpace messages and emails. One of those friends recalls the two of them in their school uniforms giddily talking about the messages. The other friend remembers being with her in her bedroom and Jade saying: “Can you believe someone like him is messaging me?”

In August 2007, a few days after Walliams turned 36, Jade, who was then 15 and five months, says he arranged to meet her at Fresh & Wild, a high-end grocery store and cafe in Soho, central London. Jade was excited. “I think when you see someone on telly, you sort of feel like you know them,” she says. “You sort of feel – well, it’ll be fine, won’t it?”

Walliams was already at a table when she arrived, she recalls, and had ordered them coffees. “He got up and gave me a hug and just sort of said hello.” Not a fan of coffee, Jade says she tried to gulp it down, as she was keen to impress him. “I was very, very shy, so I was quite quiet. So it was a lot of him sort of asking questions and things. Again, it was a bit about school, but it wasn’t long until he asked me if I’d ever had sex before.”

Embarrassed, she says, she told Walliams she had not had sex, but disclosed that she had been a victim of sexual abuse as a child. “He was all sort of: ‘Oh, I’m sorry about that,’” she says.

Jade says that after they finished their coffees, Walliams offered to walk her towards the tube station. They were walking down a sidestreet when Walliams edged her into a corner. “That’s when he kissed me.” She says the kiss was forceful and came as a surprise. She remembers he used his tongue. “I let him. I obviously kissed him back. But again, when I’m in that sort of [situation], I shut off completely.”

After the kiss, Jade says, Walliams invited her back to his house. She remembers him leading her to the car park where he had left his Aston Martin, a brand she recognised as one her father liked.

She recalls that they drove to his house in near silence. “I think I was still naive to what he wanted to happen,” she says. “I didn’t think he would want sex, especially that quickly.”

Walliams, who by then lived in a grand, five-storey townhouse in Belsize Park known as Supernova Heights, led her into its open-plan living space. Jade remembers sitting nervously on a large L-shaped sofa while Walliams leaned on a kitchen island countertop. “I just went silent,” she says, until “he asked me to come over and gave me a hug. And that’s when he kissed me again.”

She says he then lifted up her T-shirt, pulled down her bra and sucked her breast. He took her hand and started to put it down his trousers. She says she was aware that he had an erection and she pulled away. “I wasn’t ready for sex. I didn’t want to do that with him or with anyone. I was very uncomfortable with my own body as well. And I didn’t – I didn’t want to be touched in that way at all. I mean, I was only a 15-year-old.”

Walliams agreed to stop. She recalls him saying “that we should wait until I’m 16 and then said to keep in contact … I remember him saying that. That comment will always stick out in my mind. That’s a very strange thing to say.”

Lawyers for Walliams say he never engaged in grooming young women, and he denies that he had any sexual contact with Jade. They say the allegations of serious criminal conduct are false.

In the months after, Jade and Walliams continued to email each other, but she started to get the sense that Walliams was cooling off. “I think he was just trying to keep me at arm’s length a bit, but also keep me around in a way,” she says.

In February 2008, Jade spotted an article in the News of the World that featured a 20-year-old Russian model called Elizaveta Osova, who claimed Walliams had contacted her out of the blue on Facebook and had been “using me for sex”.

Jade says she felt confused and hurt to realise she was not the only one Walliams was talking to online. “So I sent [the article] to him and I was like: ‘What’s up with this?!’ And I never got a response.”

Later, Jade took friends on two occasions to see Supernova Heights, the house where she says Walliams had taken her. On one occasion, she says, she rang the buzzer, planning to confront him, but then left scared when a voice on the other end of the intercom replied.

Now that she is older, Jade considers what she says happened to her to have been sexual assault. “It’s grooming, she adds. “It’s completely wrong in every way.”

Supernova Heights came with rock’n’roll credentials. Previously owned by Noel Gallagher at the height of Oasis mania, it had become a landmark for fans, who scrawled their names and devotion to the band on the front garden wall. In the tabloid press in the early 00s, it was the symbolic centre of a group of partying celebrities nicknamed the Primrose Hill set.

Walliams bought the house in 2005 for a reported £3.25m. Interviewed for Boyd Hilton’s book Inside Little Britain, Walliams said he was worried that the house was so big that he might get lonely. He then quipped that he would rename it “Superduper Heights”. The new name never stuck, but the house kept its status as the north London hub for salacious tabloid gossip columns, now with Walliams at the heart.

In January 2008, five months after Jade says she stepped through the door, Supernova Heights was the scene of the kind of VIP soiree that tabloid columnists loved to write about: a gathering, over drinks and cupcakes, that included the comedian David Baddiel, the singer Neil Tennant from Pet Shop Boys, and Jonathan Ross. Ella had been invited with a friend. She had just turned 20; Walliams was 36.

A few weeks earlier, Ella, who was then a student and a part-time model, says she had received a voicemail from Walliams out of the blue. Unbeknownst to her, Walliams had contacted her modelling agent and asked for her number. Lawyers say Walliams understood it had been provided with her knowledge and permission. They went for dinner and then Walliams sent Ella a huge bouquet of roses to her student flat. Soon after, she says, he invited her to the party.

Ella says she was not interested in Walliams romantically, but she was “dazzled to a good degree by his fame” and was intrigued to see how a celebrity lived.

She was also confused about why Walliams was showing her so much attention. “Honestly, I thought he was probably gay,” Ella says. His camp persona caused endless speculation in the press about his sexuality. In a now highly questionable feature, the Sun regularly printed a “gay-o-meter” ranking how gay or straight Walliams was considered to be that week.

Even so, Ella and her friend both recall that at the party she intentionally acted immaturely, as a way of putting Walliams off. Ella says she felt many of Walliams’ guests seemed uncomfortable that two young women were there. “One of the guests’ wives did pull me aside at one point,” she says, “and was like, you know: ‘You’re very young, be careful.’”

As the night wore on, Ella claims that Walliams wanted more of her attention and invited her for a tour of the house. He led her upstairs. In his bedroom, she says, he invited her to look at the view out of the window. “And I remember feeling him come up really close behind me. And the hairs going up from the back of my neck,” she says. “I turned round and his hands were placed at either side of the window, and he’s a big man, he’s quite intimidating, and he leaned in for a kiss, and I just remember going ‘ugh’ and ducking underneath his arm, running away.”

She recalls sitting on a sofa later that evening, when Walliams, lying down, put his head in her lap and begged her to stay the night with him. She says she felt vulnerable in the house and calls his behaviour “emotionally manipulative and inappropriate”.

Now a mother in her 30s, Ella says she feels that the way Walliams contacted her and then pursued her at a young age was an abuse of power.

“I felt vulnerable and I felt intimidated,” she says. “My overwhelming emotion is relief. I feel really lucky. I felt like I dodged a bullet and I think it could have been a very different story.”

Walliams’ lawyers say he was hoping Ella might want to have a serious relationship with him.

They say as far as he can recall he had invited her and her friend spontaneously to attend the gathering at his house and that they were the only women present.

His lawyers say Walliams made what was intended to be a comically clumsy pass at her in the style of Mr Bean, and that he denies putting his head in her lap. They say he had no intention of intimidating her or making her feel uncomfortable.

A year after inviting Ella to his party, Walliams was photographed with a new girlfriend, Lauren Budd, an 18-year-old model. Walliams was 37. He had reportedly sent a letter to her modelling agency asking her out.

It was a period in which Walliams was regularly linked to models. A woman who spoke to the Guardian claims that the frequency with which Walliams was known to message models was something of a joke among her colleagues. Many said they found his approaches strange. One woman said Walliams was a lovely man and she had only good things to say about him.

While his relationships were still making the headlines, Walliams was forging a new chapter in his career. In October 2008, he published his first children’s book, The Boy in the Dress. It became an overnight success and more followed.

In 2010, he married another model, Lara Stone. They later had a child. Now a family man and a successful children’s author, the once notorious Lothario was on his way to becoming a national treasure.

Walliams’ status as a family-friendly entertainer was burnished in 2012 when he became a judge on Britain’s Got Talent. His camp patter and constant ribbing of the head judge, Simon Cowell, made him a fan favourite. “I hate to admit it, but he is really, really good on the show,” Cowell told Jonathan Ross on his chatshow in early 2012.

Walliams was named most popular talent show judge four times at the National Television Awards. His children’s books featured for weeks at the top of the book charts.

While his career went from strength to strength, his family life ran into trouble and in 2015 he and Stone divorced.

Behind the scenes at BGT, in work messaging groups, concerns were being raised about Walliams’ behaviour. Production staff discussed how the star judge was messaging young female runners.

One 19-year-old showed her colleagues the messages she was receiving from Walliams. “You always put a smile on my face x,” Walliams wrote. He would refer to the runner as “gorgeous” and at one point wrote “Hot” under a photo posted on Instagram of her in a group of three other women and one man. The young runner sent a screenshot of the comment to colleagues. “Erm, David’s comment on my insta of us, WTF,” she wrote.

Concerns about this behaviour pinged around a group WhatsApp chat for young staff at BGT. “He’s weird af [as fuck],” one person wrote. “250% would not be like this if the judge runner was a guy.” A second person wrote: “He actually got in trouble a few years ago for messaging a runner. So be careful.”

A male former BGT staff member says a 21-year-old female runner showed him messages in which Walliams was asking her out. “She came up to me and said: ‘What shall I do? He’s David Walliams.’”

Another BGT insider, Amy, was 24 when she was assigned to work as Walliams’ runner for a day in 2017. She alleges Walliams stared at her chest in a way that made her feel uncomfortable. Later, she recalls, she overheard him refer to her as “the one with the arse”.

She says she felt his behaviour was “predatory”.

“It made me feel small and almost disembodied,” she says. “Like I was not a person, but just a body.”

Lawyers for Walliams say he does not recall making this remark, but agree that had he done so, it would have been hurtful. They add that he denies staring at her chest or being predatory.

Responding to allegations about his contacting of young runners, they say that viewed in context the Instagram comment was clearly meant as a joke and that the term “gorgeous” was commonly used in the entertainment industry. They say Walliams has never been warned or “got into trouble” for messaging runners and deny that he behaved inappropriately and harassed young women in the workplace.

It was not only Walliams’ behaviour towards female staff members that raised concerns. Several sources questioned why Walliams was hosting young fans in his dressing room. Abby Tomlinson was 17 and a fan of BGT when she received a message out of the blue on her Twitter (now X) account in 2015. It was an invitation from Walliams, she says, to come to watch the show being filmed. She took a 13-year-old girl along with her. When they arrived, they were shown backstage to Walliams’ dressing room, where two other girls, 16 and 17, were waiting.

Tomlinson says they were left alone with Walliams without another adult present, a claim his lawyers say is misleading.

Abby is adamant and says: “It was absolutely the case, the door was shut and we were alone with him.” She says she now feels that was inappropriate. “He’s the sort of person who had obviously a lot of access to young women, teenage girls.”

Representatives for the production companies Fremantle and Syco, which produce BGT, each say that neither company had any knowledge of any of the allegations levelled at Walliams and they had never received any complaints about him. In a statement, ITV, which broadcasts the show, said it was sorry to hear of the allegations but that Fremantle confirmed that “no complaint has ever been made to them about David Walliams’ behaviour”.

Standing under the bright television lights, Sarah smiled as she posed next to the BGT judges. Walliams had spotted her 18-year-old friend in the crowd, a young woman he had been in touch with for more than a year. He had called her, Sarah and another friend up to the BGT judges’ table for a photograph.

It was February 2016 and 18-year-old Sarah was a fan of the show. “I grew up watching Britain’s Got Talent with my mum, my sister and my dad,” she says.

After the filming ended, Sarah was waiting for a train home when she says she received a direct message from Walliams on Instagram. He was inviting her and her friends back the next day, she recalls. “He was like: ‘Come to my hotel and we’ll get some food and then I’ll take you over to Britain’s Got Talent.’”

The friends met Walliams in his hotel room before the show. He ordered burgers, chips and ice-cream. Later, he took them in a taxi to the theatre where the show was being filmed. Sarah recalls feeling glamorous and excited to suddenly be inside the world of showbiz. “I was just like: ‘This is so cool,’” she says. “You know, I was 18 and I was like: ‘What the hell am I doing here?!’”

Walliams continued to message Sarah and soon after the filming he invited her to stay at his house as she was intending to come to London, where she was considering going to study. Excited to spend more time with a celebrity and curious to see how someone so rich lived, she accepted the invitation. “I said to him I’ll only come on the condition my friend also comes.” She says Walliams agreed.

Later that month, Walliams sent Sarah an email. He was 44. “Are you looking forward to next weekend…?” he wrote, signing off with a kiss. Sarah recalls thinking it would be a “fun little weekend. That was literally all I thought it was gonna be. I was so innocent.”

Sarah says Walliams booked the two 18-year-olds a spa day at the Bulgari hotel in Knightsbridge, central London. When the women checked the spa’s website, they found the prices eye-wateringly expensive.

Sarah remembers being equally impressed when they arrived at Supernova Heights. Walliams gave them the tour: the huge kitchen island, the grand bathtub in the bedroom and the awards in his office.

He made them pasta for lunch, she recalls. When Sarah got out her phone to check if there was food in her teeth, she says Walliams told her: “No photos.”

That evening, they ordered pizza, picked out some DVDs and the young women drank wine while they all stretched out on Walliams’ L-shaped sofa. Both women got progressively more drunk, Sarah says.

When she got up to go to the bathroom, Sarah remembers that Walliams followed her. She says he then put his hands around her waist and moved in to kiss her. “I had a boyfriend at the time, so I was just like: ‘Absolutely not.’” When she looked at him, she remembers thinking: “You’re the same age as my mum.”

At another point in the evening, she recalls Walliams stroking her lower leg while they were sprawled on the sofa.

The two women kept drinking. Sarah became so drunk, she says, that she struggled to walk. She alleges that Walliams took her by the arm and helped her up the stairs. The women had previously laid out their things in his two spare bedrooms. But as they passed the rooms, it became clear to Sarah that Walliams was leading her up more stairs, towards the top floor, his bedroom.

Sarah’s friend intervened, she says, and led her down the stairs to the spare room. Sarah says she remembers how, despite having drunk so much, she became suddenly on her guard. “When you’re in an environment like that and if something happens, you kind of automatically remember what’s going on.”

She believes Walliams had been taking her upstairs because he wanted something sexual to happen, despite her being inebriated and despite her having told him she was not interested. If it were not for her friend pulling her away, she believes, she would have ended up in Walliams’ bedroom.

Instead, the women slept in the spare rooms. Aged 18 and in a city they did not know, Sarah says she could not think of another option. “I could have run out the door and I wouldn’t have known where I was. I wouldn’t have known who to call. I wouldn’t have known what to do.”

In the morning, the two women started to discuss what had happened, but it felt odd to talk about it while they were in Walliams’ house. Before they left, Sarah and her friend wrote a note thanking Walliams for letting them stay and went to the Bulgari hotel spa, where she recalls an employee telling them that other female friends of Walliams had been sent there in the past.

Sarah recalls thinking at the time: “What a weird old man, like, trying his luck.”

Looking back now, at 29, she feels differently. “I think now I’m older I can realise how uncomfortable I actually was.”

She says: “If you have celebrity status, why can you not get women closer to your age range? … Is it, like, for manipulation? What do we have in common with a 44-year-old man?”

Walliams’ lawyers say he “refutes the suggestion that he got [Sarah] drunk to take advantage of her”. Although he recalls they drank wine together, they say, he does not recall anyone being drunk. They add that he did not force himself on to Sarah and that there was no sexual contact with her. Both women were friendly the next day and did not raise any issue with Walliams, they say.

The lawyers add that he denies targeting teenage women and using his celebrity status to manipulate them to have sex with him.

Eight months after the incident in the house, Sarah was walking through a supermarket when she got a call from her friend with a startling development.

The friend had remained in touch with Walliams and been to watch more BGT shows. While there, she had met two other young women whom she saw go backstage. Later, she had contacted them to tell them about what had happened in his house. And then she had received a threatening letter from Walliams’ lawyers.

The letter was written by Jenny Afia, a renowned lawyer specialising in reputation management for the law firm Schillings. Afia is best known now for representing the Duchess of Sussex. She also acted for Walliams. Afia wrote to the young woman, who was 19 at the time: “You are at a significant risk of committing a serious civil offence should you disclose, to the press or any other third party, private information or purported private information concerning our client.”

A spokesperson for Schillings said they had been instructed to write the letter as they had understood that the woman was going to “sell her story”, which Walliams believed was “an untruthful account”. Walliams’ lawyers add that he was concerned about the impact such a story could have on his family.

The legal letter demanded a written undertaking within 24 hours that the woman would not talk about her experience with Walliams. She had no representation and Sarah says she was shaken by the threat.

“If that was me, I’d have freaked out,” Sarah says. Looking back, she wonders if such action had a chilling effect on other women speaking out. “I think all this should have come out a long time ago.”

In October 2017, a year after the Schillings letter, Walliams was presented with an OBE at Buckingham Palace for services to charity and the arts. “I remind myself every day how lucky I am to be working with incredible people,” he told reporters. “I don’t take any of it for granted, especially not today.”

He continued to entertain the public on BGT and his children’s books dominated the market. Many were developed into TV and stage shows. He sold Supernova Heights and moved to a grander property.

He continued to message young women on social media. The Guardian has spoken to seven other women who say Walliams contacted them on social media platforms around this time. One was an 18-year-old college student at the time. Six were models who were between 19 and 22 when he made contact. None had a sexual encounter with him, but all the women feel the approach was odd, given Walliams was so famous.

In the course of the investigation, the Guardian and ITV News contacted more than 100 people. A few spoke positively of their interactions with Walliams, saying he was always professional and pleasant, but many expressed concerns about his behaviour towards women.

By 2020, Walliams’ contributions to culture were starting to be reassessed. In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement, his work with Little Britain was attracting criticism. The sketch show was removed from various streaming platforms over concerns about Walliams’ and Lucas’s use of blackface, something for which both men apologised.

More criticism came when a clip from Little Britain’s Australian tour in 2007 resurfaced. It captured Walliams, in character as the washed-up TV presenter Des Kaye, pulling a 16-year-old boy on to the stage and proceeding to kiss him on the lips and pull down his trousers and underwear. Walliams had been aware that the act, also performed at other shows, was controversial even at the time. In a book documenting the UK tour of the same show, Walliams was quoted as saying: “If we did the show in America, I’d probably get lawsuits from everyone I molested, but in Bournemouth I can somehow get away with it.”

His children’s books came under fire, too. In July 2020, the activist and food writer Jack Monroe posted a viral thread on Twitter criticising them as “sneering classist fatshaming nonsense”.

The day after that post came a series of tweets from Sarah’s friend who had met Walliams backstage at BGT and stayed in his house. In the posts, which went viral, she wrote: “Why did I ever think it was ‘normal’ for a 44yr male to invite four girls aged 16/17 into his dressing room without any adults – just his PA, who would bring refreshments once in a while. And the fact that everyone at that TV production company would see it and say NOTHING.”

Inside the offices of his then publisher, HarperCollins, the tweets from Monroe and Sarah’s friend were a cause for concern among staff. Several people remember managers reassuring them that the flurry of criticism on Twitter would pass.

Signed to HarperCollins in 2008, Walliams was one of the publisher’s biggest success stories. For years, his titles were the bestselling books in the publisher’s catalogue. He has sold more than 26m copies in the UK alone, worth £156m.

Several employees suggested this success protected him for years.

In 2017, Walliams was introduced to an intern in her mid-20s. They met at a promotional event at a school. Walliams was 45. The young woman was later sent to Walliams’ house alone and they began what Walliams’ lawyers describe a “consensual sexual” relationship. At one point, Walliams sent her flowers to the office.

The young woman later said that although consensual, looking back she felt the relationship was an “abuse of power”, according to multiple sources.

Around the office, women started to warn each other not to go to Walliams’ house alone.

Katie, a former employee, says she went to HR after a young colleague in her mid-20s showed her messages that Walliams had been sending her, in which he was asking her out.

He had met that young woman at a promotional event at a school for World Book Day, then had obtained her email address and invited her to dinner. The woman ignored the email. Months later, he tried again.

“It’s just not appropriate for an author to be messaging a member of staff like that. She definitely wasn’t pleased about it,” Katie says.

Lawyers for Walliams say he messaged the young woman at a time when he was “heartbroken and lonely after his divorce and was hoping to meet someone to spend time with”.

More concerns bounced around the HarperCollins’ office when, in 2022, the Guardian reported on derogatory and sexually explicit remarks that Walliams had made about contestants on BGT. The story caused a storm. Walliams apologised and said they were private conversations. Nevertheless, it was the first time the media had reported on his inappropriate conduct and it led to him being dropped as a judge after 10 years on the show.

Around the same time, the children’s section of HarperCollins brought in a new head, Cally Poplak. After hearing concerns about Walliams’ alleged inappropriate behaviour from staff members, Poplak initiated an inquiry in late 2023. At least five female members of staff discussed their experiences and managers were told about the sexual relationship Walliams had with the junior employee.

The investigation wrapped up in 2024 with no consequences for Walliams. For one woman who spoke to the inquiry, it was the end of her career at the company. She was reportedly given a five-figure payout and signed a separation agreement with a strict non-disclosure clause.

For nearly two years after the investigation concluded, the company continued to publish Walliams’ books, only dropping him in December last year after a change of management. He said at the time that the issues raised in the inquiry were never brought to his attention.

Then, in September, it was announced that it would no longer publish any of his works.

Lawyers for Walliams say he denies the allegations of sexual harassment and inappropriate behaviour in the workplace.

At the time, a HarperCollins spokesperson said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that they took “employee wellbeing extremely seriously”. When approached for this investigation, they said they could add nothing further.

When news broke that Walliams had been dropped by his publisher, many of the women he had had encounters with held their breath. Some thought this would be the catalyst for detailed allegations to come out. But there was no moment of reckoning.

For some of the women who have encountered Walliams over the years, the silence left them angry.

Jade, who said she had met up with Walliams when she was 15, is now a mother. She has banned her younger children from bringing his books home from school. “And I look at my daughter, who’s not far off [being 15] now, and to think of a 36-year-old man being any way like that with her makes me feel sick,” she says.

“It angers me that he is still on the TV, as famous as he is. He used that fame to get women.”

Several names have been changed at the request of sources.

The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse, childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

#195. Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly

Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.

Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.

A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.

The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator. At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.

Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs, is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.

The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.

Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.

“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere. We’re just going to see how people use it, what they’re trying to do, and keep showing more. We don’t have any need or desire to sort of limit what the MCP endpoint can expose. What we really want to do is to support that creative workflow, how you choose to do it,” said Subramaniam.

Last month, Adobe rival Figma co-founder Dylan Field said at an event in India that MCP is not a perfect standard and benefits frontier labs more.

#191. US evacuates aircraft from RAF Mildenhall over reported Iran threat

Move comes weeks after Washington withdrew bombers from RAF Fairford after a suspected security incident

Several US military aircraft were evacuated from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk on Monday, after the US Air Force concluded they could be at risk from a possible Iranian threat if they remained at the British base.

Ten air tankers were relocated to bases in Germany, Spain and Scotland, while Osprey transport aircraft were sent to nearby RAF Lakenheath. It is the second time the US has undertaken a hasty redeployment in the UK with some of its bombers pulled from RAF Fairford in October.

The latest incident was said to be in response to a threat from Iran, according to the Wall Street Journal, although British sources emphasised there was no immediate or direct danger to the base or the area nearby.

Washington withdrew B-1 bombers from the Fairford base just over a month ago – a week after ⁠a suspected Iran-linked ​security incident in September. Two men have been charged with espionage offences on behalf of Iran after the episode.

The precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains ⁠under discussion among US officials, and the Pentagon has chosen to take a risk averse approach when it receives threats to planes on the ground after the first phase of the Iran war in the spring.

Five KC-135 Stratotankers, the same refuelling aircraft moved out of Mildenhall, were hit on the ground by an Iranian missile in Saudi Arabia in March, and the US is concerned about how well planes are protected on the ground.

UK security officials however believe that Iran does not have the capability to launch an explosive attack on a base in the UK, although Tehran may threaten to do so in an attempt to disrupt American military calculations.

Donald Trump, the US president, is considering whether to renew the bombing of Iran, although overnight he said further attacks were “highly unlikely” in the aftermath of last week’s midterm elections, when his Republican party was heavily defeated. Trump allies, including the vice-president, JD Vance, blamed the war for the poor results.

Luke Pollard, a British junior defence minister, told a military conference in Oslo “it was a decision for the US where they place their military assets” and that the UK was “investing more” in counter-drone capabilities and base protection.

Local residents are being advised to remain vigilant in case of any untoward developments in the vicinity of Mildenhall or other bases used by the US air force in the UK, though it was not said they faced any heightened risk.

However, the US had reportedly upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath on Monday,according to a US ‌official familiar with the ‌matter.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

The base was placed under Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, which is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system ‌and occurs when intelligence indicates a form of terrorist action is likely.

A US Air Force spokesperson said: “US Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons, including training and real world requirements. US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”

Five men driving three white vans were arrested at a village outside RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire shortly after midnight on 27 September over a suspected plot to attack the base. Although a bomb warning had been made, no explosives were found in the search and the men were released on bail.

A month later two men were charged with assisting Iranian intelligence in the relation to the incident under the National Security Act 2023, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24. Essghir was one of the five who was initially arrested near the airbase, while Abdulkarim is accused of buying the vans.

While Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied accusations it was involved in any plot against the airbase, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that Fairford and any other bases used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

#186. Pharma firms’ focus on weight-loss drugs could put insulin supply at risk, experts warn

GLP-1 products such as Ozempic and Mounjaro spread but many in poorer countries struggle to get basic diabetes treatment

The gold rush into GLP-1 weight-loss drugs risks diverting pharmaceutical firms’ attention away from diabetes treatments such as insulin, the head of the Access to Medicine Foundation has warned.

GLP-1 blockbuster medications such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro have revolutionised obesity and diabetes treatment but there has been a greater focus by companies on weight loss, according to a report from the Netherlands-based non-profit group.

The group warned that many people cannot even get hold of basic insulin, critical for people with type 1 diabetes, and many countries are struggling to access GLP-1 medications at all – as the explosion in their popularity continues since the weight-loss jab Wegovy launched in 2021.

Diabetes affects an estimated 589 million adults globally, 81% of whom live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Pakistan, Egypt and Jordan.

“A lot of the GLP-1 drugs are just starting to enter these LMIC markets for obesity,” said Jay Iyer, the foundation’s chief executive, adding: “You have a lot of attention on GLP-1s, but a lot of it is directed towards the obesity market, and that’s not going to help people with type 1 diabetes who after 105 years of insulin development still do not have access to the drug.

Companies are able to charge far higher prices and enjoy greater profit margins on weight loss injections and pills, compared with other medication such as insulin.

“There is a risk that any of the three – Sanofi, [Eli] Lilly or Novo [Nordisk]– could leave the insulin market, and that will be disastrous for supply to insulin especially for people living with type 1 diabetes and insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes.”

Novo Nordisk has announced plans to phase out some of its older diabetes products, including insulin pens.

GLP-1 medications are not registered in many lower-income countries and even where they are available, their high price and companies’ lack of equitable pricing measures mean they are out of reach for most people in those places.

The drugs were initially developed to manage type 2 diabetes by regulating blood sugar, slowing digestion and reducing appetite, but their growing use for obesity has opened up a huge, lucrative market for pharmaceutical companies. GLP-1s are taken by millions of people in the US and other wealthy countries.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

The biennial report by the Access to Medicine Foundation – which is part-funded by the UK and Dutch governments – found that most of the medications being developed in this area focus on type 2 diabetes, and only 10 of the 25 target type 1 diabetes.

Switzerland’s Novartis came top of its global health equity ranking again after knocking the UK’s GSK off the top spot last time, while fellow British drugmaker AstraZeneca moved up to third place, with access plans for almost all its drugs in late-stage development.

Nearly two-thirds of cancer drugs are covered by measures to make them available in poorer countries. Looking back over the last 20 years of the access to medicines index, Iyer said progress had been made and access is now considered a part of corporate strategy at some companies, and is sometimes included in executive bonus targets.

#185. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#179. Cop31 live: host Turkey celebrates new oilfields as climate summit enters second day

Host Turkey celebrates new oilfields as UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night.

“We have discovered oil in two further fields in the region. Production began in October at the fields we have named Gaziler and Çardaklı. According to our initial assessments, these two new fields hold an in-situ oil potential of 135m barrels.”

The new fields and further wells should increase oil production by 30% in the Gabar region, which has “virtually become the capital of oil”, Erdoğan said in separate comments made after a cabinet meeting yesterday.

Burning fossil fuels is the main driver of carbon pollution and the resultant heating of the planet, and roadmaps to a clean economy require steep, immediate cuts to the supply of coal, oil and gas.

Turkey is far from alone in expanding fossil fuel infrastructure while promising climate action. In recent weeks, co-host Australia granted a licence to restart production at an offshore gasfield, the UK gave the green light to the already-licenced Jackdaw gasfield, and Norway announced a new oil and gas discovery in the North Sea.

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”

In comments reported by AP, she told reporters in Antalya: “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority, and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.

Cop31 is the first UN climate summit Thunberg has attended since the Cop26 conference in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”

Since then, fossil fuel emissions have continued to rise – though they flatlined this year – adding even more planet-heating gas to a beleaguered atmosphere. While many big polluters have taken steps to clean up their economies, none are doing so fast enough to keep global heating to the 1.5C Paris climate target.

Here’s a video of Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and president of the Cop31 negotiations, making the case for working together – and the benefits of doing so – at the opening of the summit yesterday. (Subtitles are on.)

Turkey’s celebration of the discovery of two new oilfields last night is already raising eyebrows. While Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s language is more restrained than that of his Azerbaijani counterpart, President Ilham Aliyev, two years ago – when he called oil and gas a “gift from God” at the Cop29 summit – it clashes directly with the strategies to phase out fossil fuels being discussed in Antalya today.

Jeni Miller, head of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a network of more than 300 health groups addressing climate change, said it sends a “deeply troubling message” to communities where lives, homes and futures are already at stake from climate change and fossil fuel pollution.

“The message from Turkey could not be more contradictory,” said Miller. “How can a country host the world’s most important climate conference – with Cop31 President, Murat Kurum, calling for stronger health systems to protect people from the climate crisis as part of the Antalya Initiative for Resilient Health Systems (AIR) – and on the same day announce plans to expand production of the fossil fuels driving that crisis”

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

I’ve been interviewing some of the young climate activists who have gone to the summit. Today I spoke to Yania Hussain Ishan, an 18-year-old climate activist attending Cop31 with the Maldives youth delegation.

She joined a Unicef climate programme at 16 and went on to found Barnacles, a climate initiative working to connect young people.

“Growing up in the Maldives has shaped the way I understand climate change. It’s difficult to separate it from everyday life when so much of what makes our home what it is depends on our environment. I’ve seen how coastlines change, how waves reach roads and public spaces, how flooding affects businesses near the shore, and how rough seas can disrupt the journeys that connect our islands. These are things you grow up seeing, but as you get older, you start thinking a little more about what they mean for the future.

“Sometimes I wonder what the Maldives will look like when I’m older, or what it will be like for children growing up here 20 or 30 years from now. Will they get to experience the same things we did? Will the places we grew up with still feel the same? I don’t think these are questions young people should have to spend so much time worrying about, but for many of us, they’re difficult to ignore.

“At Cop31, I hope we can move beyond repeatedly acknowledging how vulnerable countries like ours are and start paying closer attention to what actually needs to happen. Climate finance, adaptation and loss and damage have very real implications for the lives people get to lead. I also hope young people are given opportunities to meaningfully influence these conversations, rather than simply being invited to participate.

“I think about my own future and what the Maldives will look like by the time I’m older. I want to be able to build my life here, and I want the generations after me to have that same opportunity. I want them to experience the Maldives in all the ways that make it home to us, rather than having to learn about what it once was.”

The death toll from an explosion at a steelworks in western Turkey yesterday has risen to 17 people, Turkish officials have said.

The blast and fire ripped through the iron and steel factory in Aliağa, near Izmir, about 400km northwest of Antalya, on Monday.

In comments reported by AFP, the provincial governor, Suleyman Elban, said a crane fell into a furnace as it was replacing a boiler, which led to an explosion in a nearby steel mill.

The Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, offered condolences to the grieving families yesterday, when 16 people were thought to have lost their lives. The death toll has since risen to 17.

Now the former US secretary of state, John Kerry, has joined the calls for Cop31 to pick up the mantle of building support to transition away from fossil fuels.

“We are going to have to draw on ourselves and find the courage to speak the truth to powerful interests that seem intent to ignore the basic science.

“We know clean power is cheaper than fossil power. That argument is over except amongst those people who keep wanting to hold on to the past.”

Then the UN secretary general is excused from the stage to attend another meeting, and the room gives him a raucous standing ovation as he walks out.

We’ve just heard from Patricia Espinosa, the former UN climate boss (succeeded by Simon Stiell) and now we are hearing from former US secretary of state and climate ambassador, John Kerry.

Kerry has congratulated Brazil for keeping the fossil fuel transition issue alive, and the room has erupted in cheers.

We’re in the plenary that’s promoting Brazil’s new roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, and the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, has backed up the comments of the UN secretary general a few moments ago. Perhaps not unexpected, given Guterres is his boss. But he said:

“Antalya must accelerate delivery [of a transition away from fossil fuels]. This roadmap can help us do that.”.

The UN secretary-general, António Guterres, has just issued a challenge to Turkey and Australia to carry on the work to develop a roadmap for the plan to transition away from fossil fuels.

Remember that this roadmap, promoted by last year’s Cop president, Brazil, is not even on the official agenda here at Cop31.

We might see this as an intervention. Guterres said:

“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it. I thank the Presidency for its leadership.

“Let us leave Antalya with clear next steps to advance this Roadmap. I encourage the current and future Cop Presidencies to carry this work forward. We must give the world reason to believe in the commitment made at Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels.”

This will need a response from Australia and Turkey.

The president of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil, the veteran Brazilian diplomat André Aranha Corrêa do Lago, is presenting his roadmap for “Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Energy Systems” on a stage here in Antalya.

Alongside him is the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, former US secretary of state, John Kerry, and British conservative politician, Lord Alok Sharma, who was the president of Cop26 in Glasgow.

A pretty remarkable lineup. The very large plenary room is packed.

A short update on our Cop31 bus journey from hell.

We have arrived. It only took three and a half hours. And it turned out I had the key for our Guardian Cop31 media cubicle, which meant my colleagues had to do some wrangling to get inside.

But to show they bore no grudges and, as a testament to the collegiate and supportive spirit that exists within the Guardian’s Cop31 reporting team, here is what greeted me at my desk after my odyssey.

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night.

“We have discovered oil in two further fields in the region. Production began in October at the fields we have named Gaziler and Çardaklı. According to our initial assessments, these two new fields hold an in-situ oil potential of 135m barrels.”

The new fields and further wells should increase oil production by 30% in the Gabar region, which has “virtually become the capital of oil”, Erdoğan said in separate comments made after a cabinet meeting yesterday.

Burning fossil fuels is the main driver of carbon pollution and the resultant heating of the planet, and roadmaps to a clean economy require steep, immediate cuts to the supply of coal, oil and gas.

Turkey is far from alone in expanding fossil fuel infrastructure while promising climate action. In recent weeks, co-host Australia granted a licence to restart production at an offshore gasfield, the UK gave the green light to the already-licenced Jackdaw gasfield, and Norway announced a new oil and gas discovery in the North Sea.

Bus horror update. So I am still on the bus and it has been three hours. We think we are still half an hour away (I said that an hour ago).

Some people got off and tried the tram. Splitters. We watched a packed tram go past and leave a few of the splitters on the platform.

Some people are walking. We are now a forming a community forged in bus hell. Philippa has some Simit – like a Turkish bagel. Here’s a picture of us.

Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

In an attempt to get to the venue a bit early, I decided to ditch the tram and try the special Cop31 buses. This was a bad decision.

We have just reached the two-and-a-half-hour mark on the bus and are still crawling through Antalya traffic. New friendships are being spawned in here. We are starting to eat each other’s food.

I want to thank Philippa Bayley from Groundwork for the walnut and chocolate biscuits she snaffled from her hotel buffet.

Exceptional, which is more than I can say for the traffic.

Good morning from Turkey and welcome to the second day of Cop31, the UN gathering that is taking place, again, to help prod indolent countries clear of catastrophic planetary heating.

A lot of angst was vented on the first day of the summit over whether this goal is being achieved, and even if Cop is the best forum in which to achieve it. Perhaps sensing the fractured, distracted geopolitical mood, Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and Cop negotiations chief, plaintively urged countries to “show the world that multilateralism works. Let’s show the world we are equal to the challenge.”

Further evidence, if it was needed, was unveiled yesterday showing the world is failing rather badly in this challenge to stem its growing fever. But research published this morning shows carbon emissions from fossil fuels are falling slightly, and there is still hope here in Antalya that things can change. If not then, well, what are we all doing here? Right?

About 100,000 delegates crammed into the well-tended conference venue yesterday and the long queues for registration badges led the UN to plead for people to return for them today if attendance on Monday wasn’t compulsory.

Tuesday will lay the groundwork for the arrival tomorrow of leaders from more than 90 countries, with notable absentees including the heads of the US and China. Today’s theme is “energy and transport, touching on a key goal of this Cop to get the world to agree to greatly increase the share of energy used via electricity”. That power will, hopefully, be clean.

Let’s see how close to consensus the world will be on that. At the very least, the Turkish baked goods promise to be delicious and there is some tasteful art constructed of discarded waste to look at. Onwards.

#176. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.
